## 2026-05-16 - BE-0037
- What was implemented: the canonical pagination contract every customer-facing
  list endpoint will compose — limit/cursor/sort/filter parsing with stable
  apierr.InvalidInput violations, an opaque base64url cursor with a stable
  internal schema, and the Page[T] envelope (items + next_cursor +
  total_estimate) that goes inside the existing yalla.output.v1 success
  envelope.
  - internal/controlplane/pagination/pagination.go (new): package doc, the
    DefaultLimit=50 / MaxLimit=200 / MinLimit=1 constants, the SortDirection
    enum (asc/desc with IsValid()), the ParseOptions struct that an endpoint
    constructs once at handler construction time (DefaultLimit, MaxLimit,
    DefaultSort, DefaultDirection, SortAllowList, FilterAllowList), and
    ParseParams(url.Values, ParseOptions) (Params, error). ParseParams
    accumulates every violation into a single apierr.InvalidInput envelope
    (e.g. limit=0 + direction=sideways returns ONE 400 with two field
    violations, not a partial result), enforces the package MaxLimit ceiling
    even when an endpoint misconfigures its own (effectiveMaxLimit clamps),
    and the violation Reason text NEVER echoes the submitted value — only
    classification + accepted range — so a caller cannot reflect arbitrary
    content into the error message. Filter parsing strips the "filter."
    prefix, rejects unknown keys + empty/whitespace values, and trims valid
    values.
  - internal/controlplane/pagination/cursor.go (new): Cursor struct
    (Position + Sort + Direction), IsZero(), and EncodeCursor/DecodeCursor.
    Wire format: base64url-encoded JSON {v: "yalla.cursor.v1", p, s, d} —
    cursorSchemaVersion sentinel guards against fuzzed-base64 admit attacks
    and reserves a future cursor schema bump. EncodeCursor is deterministic
    (same input -> same encoding so HTTP fixtures diff byte-for-byte) and
    URL-safe (RawURLEncoding, no '+/=' so it does not need percent-encoding).
    DecodeCursor accepts both padded and unpadded base64 (some log pipelines
    add padding); empty input resolves to the zero cursor with no error so
    handlers branch uniformly on Cursor.IsZero. Every failure mode (invalid
    base64, invalid JSON, unknown schema_version, empty Position, malformed
    direction) collapses to a single errMalformedCursor sentinel —
    DecodeCursor never returns a typed code, ParseParams wraps it as a
    stable FieldViolation on the "cursor" field, so the wire contract
    survives a future cursor-internal change.
  - internal/controlplane/pagination/page.go (new): the Page[T any] generic
    envelope (Items []T json:"items" — always non-nil per BuildPage,
    NextCursor string json:"next_cursor,omitempty" — empty means end of
    stream, TotalEstimate *int64 json:"total_estimate,omitempty" — pointer
    so absent (nil/omitted) is distinguishable from zero rows on endpoints
    that do not compute it cheaply). BuildPage[T any](rows, limit,
    position, totalEstimate) implements the over-fetch trim: the store
    fetches Limit+1 rows, BuildPage retains Limit and encodes next_cursor
    from the last retained row's Position via a PositionFunc[T] adapter.
    BuildPage never returns nil Items and tolerates a misconfigured
    limit<MinLimit by clamping (does not panic).
  - internal/controlplane/pagination/pagination_test.go (new): 17 tests
    covering ParseParams defaults, endpoint-provided overrides,
    MaxLimit-ceiling clamping (an endpoint that asks for MaxLimit*2 still
    only gets MaxLimit), four bad-?limit= classifications (non-numeric,
    zero, negative, too-large) each asserted to NOT echo the submitted
    value, unknown-sort rejection, allow-listed-sort acceptance, bad-
    direction rejection, unknown-filter-key rejection, empty-filter-value
    rejection, allow-listed-filter trimming, malformed-cursor rejection,
    cursor sort-mismatch rejection, cursor direction-mismatch rejection,
    multi-violation accumulation, valid-cursor acceptance, the
    SortDirection enum validator, and the effectiveDefaultLimit clamping
    table.
  - internal/controlplane/pagination/cursor_test.go (new): 12 tests
    covering IsZero, EncodeCursor/DecodeCursor round trip, empty-cursor
    semantics, encode determinism over 16 iterations, URL-safety (no
    "+/="), the opacity guarantee (the plaintext Position string does NOT
    appear as a substring in the encoded form), malformed-base64
    rejection, malformed-JSON rejection, unknown-schema-version
    rejection, empty-Position rejection, malformed-direction rejection,
    both-padding-forms decode, AND the load-bearing tenant-isolation
    contract guard: TestDecodeCursorTenantIsolationCannotBeBypassed
    decodes a synthetic cursor payload into a generic map and asserts
    NONE of {organization_id, org_id, tenant, tenant_id, principal,
    principal_id} are keys — adding one is now impossible without
    breaking the suite, which freezes the contract "cursor never carries
    a tenant identifier; tenant isolation is the persistence layer's
    responsibility".
  - internal/controlplane/pagination/page_test.go (new): 9 tests covering
    BuildPage's never-nil Items invariant, under-limit retention, over-
    fetch trim + next_cursor encoding, TotalEstimate forwarding, zero-
    limit non-panic, full-set traversal without duplicates across many
    pages (a 10-row / pageSize=3 paging-end-to-end test asserts every
    row appears exactly once across all pages and the final page has
    NextCursor==""), cursor stability under concurrent inserts
    (TestCursorIsStableUnderInserts: seed 6 rows, page once, insert
    "r10" and "r11" with larger createdAt AFTER page 1 was served, page
    2 returns exactly the 3 remaining originals — no duplicates, no
    skips, the newly-inserted rows do NOT leak onto page 2 because the
    cursor is a strict upper bound on the (sort_key DESC, id DESC)
    composite key), tenant isolation under cursor paging
    (TestCursorTenantIsolation: two organizations seeded with identical
    row ids, paging org_a end to end never observes an org_b row, AND a
    cursor produced from org_a paged against the store as org_b only
    yields org_b's rows — the cursor only encodes a position, the
    store layer's organization_id filter is authoritative), and a
    tampered-cursor rejection through ParseParams.

- Remaining risks or follow-ups:
  - Existing list endpoints (GET /v1/organizations/{org_id}/audit-events

    list endpoints) predate this contract and still use bespoke

    Each is a separate migration story; BE-0037 is intentionally
    additive (no behavior change to those endpoints).
  - No store-layer cursor decoder helper yet — endpoints today should
    treat cursor.Position as the row id of the last returned row, but
    a future story can add a typed pagination/store helper for the
    canonical "ORDER BY (sort_key, id) DESC, WHERE (sort_key, id) <
    (cursor_sort, cursor_id) LIMIT ?+1" query template once two

- Learnings for future iterations:
  - Pattern: foundational contract package (no net/http import, no
    store import, no resource-specific type) — composes cleanly into
    every list endpoint without locking the package into one shape.
    Future contract stories (idempotency-key contract, ETag contract,
    request-ID contract) should follow the same shape: a small typed
    package under internal/controlplane/<name> that handlers compose,
    plus the package's own test suite that proves the contract
    standalone before any endpoint adopts it.
  - Gotcha: ctx_execute sandbox rejects /Users/juribadev/projects/poc/yalla
    as a "system temp root" and ignores go.mod, so go vet/test must
    run through the Bash tool, not the sandbox. Documented for future
    iterations.
  - Generics + Go 1.21+ builtin min: the standard library now exposes
    a builtin min; defining a local helper shadows it and is
    unnecessary. Use the builtin directly. (Caught and removed during
    implementation.)
  - The opacity test (TestEncodeCursorIsOpaque) does NOT prove
    cryptographic opacity — base64url is reversible — but it pins the
    contract that an agent cannot recover the plaintext position
    with a naive substring check. The TENANT-ISOLATION guarantee is
    structural (no tenant id in the payload), not cryptographic.
    Documented in cursor_test.go so a future change cannot blur the
    distinction.
  - Accumulating field violations is a real ergonomic win for agents:
    one POST with a bad limit AND a bad direction returns BOTH
    violations in one envelope, not a partial result that the agent
    has to re-submit twice. apierr.InvalidInput sorts the violations
    deterministically so the error message stays diff-stable across
    runs.
  - The cursor stability test (TestCursorIsStableUnderInserts) is the
    contract guarantee an AI agent depends on: "if I page through a
    list, an insert by another caller does not duplicate or skip a
    row I have already seen". The test models a fake in-memory store
    with the same ORDER BY composite key the production stores will
    use (created_at DESC, id DESC), so the contract is proven against
    the same shape repositories will adopt.

## 2026-05-16 - BE-0183 - Add policy matrix coverage for POST /v1/environments/{environment_id}/services
- What was implemented: Authorization-matrix tests for POST
  /v1/environments/{environment_id}/services. Drives every built-in
  role (owner/admin/developer/viewer/ci/support) through real
  NewHandler + real policy.NewEngine() to prove CapWrite splits the
  matrix (Owner/Admin/Developer allow via ReasonAllowedByRole;
  Viewer/CI/Support deny via ReasonDeniedNoCapability — CI is
  CapSelf+CapRead+CapDeploy, Support is CapSelf+CapRead+CapSupport,
  neither holds CapWrite). Pins revoked/expired credentials as
  Disabled-principal denials (underlying Owner role would otherwise
  allow). Pins the wrong-organization principal: a same-tenant
  resource on the wire (env_id alone never widens to another tenant)
  surfaces as a 404 from the persistence layer, never 201 (no
  foreign-environment commit) and never 403 (would confirm
  existence); the engine cross-tenant clause is exercised separately
  for every role including Support, all denied via
  ReasonDeniedCrossTenant — CapWrite is OUTSIDE the support
  cross-tenant exception, the load-bearing distinction from BE-0180.
  Pins scoped-grant containment: every project-/environment-/service-
  scoped grant is denied OutOfScope at this route because
  environmentIDResolver pins NO ProjectID leg and the engine's
  covers() rule is one-way (a grant scope that pins ProjectID cannot
  cover a resource scope that does not), even when the grant names
  the target environment's own project or own id; an org-level
  Viewer grant (CapRead-only) is denied NoCapability while an
  org-level Developer grant (CapWrite) is allowed end-to-end.

    BE-0189 (PATCH), BE-0192 (DELETE), BE-0195 (POST .../restore),
    BE-0198 (GET .../rendered), BE-0201 (GET .../variables), BE-0204
    (PUT .../variables), BE-0207 (POST .../deployments), BE-0210
    (GET .../deployments) are the remaining p=1 service-policy
    stories. They differ from BE-0183 in resolver shape: a
    {service_id}-rooted route resolves into a service resource (the
    grant-containment matrix flips — a service-scoped grant at the
    target service_id IS in scope; a project-scoped grant is in
    scope by covers() one-way), and the cross-tenant property still
    pivots on capability tier (CapRead admits Support, CapWrite/
    CapDeploy do not).

    store-backed orchestrator's parent-environment existence check
    has its own integration coverage. This story adds no new
    runtime behavior — only assertions.
- Learnings for future iterations:
  - For an env-id-rooted CapWrite POST policy matrix, the BE-0153
    pattern (POST /v1/projects/{project_id}/environments) is the
    nearest parallel for the role-split and cross-tenant deny
    structure, and BE-0180 (GET .../services) is the nearest parallel
    for the env-id-resolver scoped-grant containment shape (no
    ProjectID leg on the resource scope -> all scoped grants denied
    OutOfScope, including the same-id env grant). Combine the two:
    role split + capability deny tier from BE-0153, scoped-grant
    OutOfScope shape from BE-0180. The load-bearing engine assertion
    that distinguishes the two routes is that an org-level Viewer
    grant is allowed for service.read (BE-0180) and denied
    NoCapability for service.create (BE-0183) — the grant SCOPE is
    sufficient in both, but the grant ROLE's capability set is not
    for CapWrite. Pin both at the engine so a future catalog change
    in either direction (downgrading service.create to CapRead,
    upgrading service.read to CapWrite) fails before regressing a
    real customer.
  - The engine's cross-tenant clause is gated on
    `required == CapRead || required == CapSupport`; for any
    CapWrite/CapDeploy/CapAdmin/CapOwner action, the deny path
    extends to Support too. Always pin the role-split deny and the
    cross-tenant deny separately — they fail for different reasons
    (NoCapability when same-tenant, CrossTenant when foreign-tenant)
    and a regression in either branch should fail in exactly one
    place.
  - For env-id-resolver routes, the same-id env grant (a scoped
    grant naming the very environment the path names) is STILL
    denied OutOfScope because the grant scope pins ProjectID and the
    resource scope does not — covers() is one-way. Pin this case
    explicitly so a future relaxation that allowed env_X grants to
    cover {EnvID=env_X} resource scopes would fail before it could
    regress a real customer.

- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - The bare-id lookup-by-id vertical for a deep resource (env, svc,
    deployment) collapses to: store repo GetByID under
    (organization_id, id), reader wrapper GetXxx wrapping it in a
    short-lived Store.Read, narrow httpapi port (ServiceReader,
    distinct from EnvironmentServiceReader so a handler change to
    one doesn't ripple), bare-id resolver pinning only
    OrganizationID + the resource's ID leg (no ProjectID leg, no
    EnvironmentID leg — the load-bearing distinction from
    parent-scoped resolvers), and the existing wire-shape projection
    (environmentServiceOf for service). NewHandler/newRouteTable
    grow ONE positional port at the tail of the relevant resource
    group (right before `breakGlass`); the call-site sweep handles
    the three anchor patterns plus a handful of port-substituted
    outliers where a `reader`/`creator`/`ctl` variable sits in the
    position the sweep anchors on. Forward-applicable to BE-0213
    (GET /v1/deployments/{deployment_id}), and the same shape
    underpins the PATCH/DELETE/POST sub-action stories that follow
    on this resource.
  - The ServiceReader port for the bare-id GET reuses the same
    production *store.ServiceReader instance the parent-scoped
    EnvironmentServiceReader uses. One *store.ServiceReader
    satisfies both interfaces because the methods are structurally
    distinct (GetService vs ListEnvironmentServices) and the
    interface boundary is narrow per-handler — the wiring threads
    the same value through both positional slots in cmd/yalla-api.
    The HTTP boundary keeps the two interfaces SEPARATE (so a
    handler change to one doesn't ripple through the other and so
    fake replacement is per-route), but the production wiring
    collapses them into one constructor and one read-only
    transaction lifecycle. Forward-applicable to every future
    parent-scoped vs bare-id pair (EnvironmentReader vs the future
    EnvironmentByIDReader equivalent, ProjectReader vs the future
    ProjectByIDReader equivalent, etc.).
  - serviceIDResolver pins NO ProjectID leg and NO EnvironmentID
    leg on the resource scope, even though the underlying
    store.Service row carries both. This is intentional — the policy
    boundary is built from the principal's HOME org and the PATH
    service_id, NEVER from the row's parent ids (which the
    authorize step has not yet read). The scoped-grant deny
    property (environment-scoped Admin grant naming THIS service's
    parent environment is denied) is structurally identical to
    BE-0156's env-id-resolver shape and the same load-bearing
    distinction applies: the engine's covers() rule is one-way, and
    a grant scope pinning a ProjectID cannot cover a resource scope
    that does not.
  - First user of `tagServices = "services"`. Future GET
    /v1/deployments/{deployment_id} will introduce `tagDeployments`;
    future jobs, previews, backups endpoints each get their own
    top-level tag. The convention from this story: a top-level
    resource that owns its own bare-id route family gets its own
    OpenAPI tag (singular, lower-kebab, listed in alphabetical
    order in the tag-const block).
  - The full call-site sweep across 44 test files was driven by a

## 2026-05-16 - BE-0187
- What was implemented: PATCH /v1/services/{service_id} — the
  partial-update endpoint for the bare top-level service id route,
  the structural sibling of BE-0157 (PATCH /v1/environments/

  BE-0181 (POST) and BE-0184 (GET-by-id), unblocking BE-0188 (the

  - internal/controlplane/store/service.go: added
    ServiceRepository.Update(ctx, tx, Service, *ifMatchVersion) plus
    classifyServiceConcurrencyMiss. Update is tenant-scoped at the
    SQL predicate (organization_id = $1 AND id = $2), supports the
    optional optimistic-concurrency precondition (the second WHERE
    leg version = $5 when ifMatchVersion != nil), and only writes
    slug + display_name — kind and the parent project/environment
    are structural identity and not mutable through this surface.
    The services_bump_version trigger from migration 0011 owns the
    version column. The concurrency-miss disambiguator runs a read
    on the same *Tx to distinguish row-gone (NotFound) from
    stale-version (ConflictStale with the row's authoritative
    version), with a Internal-coded safety net if the read sees the
    same version that just failed the WHERE.
  - internal/controlplane/store/serviceservice.go: added
    serviceUpdateAction = "service.update", UpdateServiceInput

    /v1/environments/{environment_id}) ports cleanly to services
    with mechanical substitutions: environment→service everywhere
    in the store and httpapi layers, ActionEnvironmentUpdate
    →ActionServiceUpdate, environmentUpdateAction
    →serviceUpdateAction, environmentIDResolver
    →serviceIDResolver, EnvironmentUpdater→ServiceUpdater,
    UpdateEnvironmentInput→UpdateServiceInput,
    buildEnvironmentUpdate→buildServiceUpdate,
    validateEnvironmentDisplayName→validateServiceDisplayName,
    classifyEnvironmentConcurrencyMiss
    →classifyServiceConcurrencyMiss. The fixture is canonical at
    this point: the SAME pattern will repeat for DELETE (BE-0190)
    and the POST sub-actions (restore, deployments, restart,
    stop, start, rollback) — each just changes the action and
    the in-flight state machine guard.
  - The "thread a new positional port through NewHandler" pattern
    now has a stable mechanical sweep:
    1. add the port interface in the resource's httpapi file;
    2. add the parameter to newRouteTable (between the resource's
       previous port and breakGlass);
    3. add the parameter to NewHandler and forward it to
       newRouteTable;
    4. add the wire call in cmd/yalla-api/main.go;
    5. sweep every test file's NewHandler call to insert
       fakeXxx{} at the new positional slot;
    6. patch the outliers — variables in port positions (reader,
       ctl, updater) and the rare trailing logger,nil callsite
       (services_test.go line 398 in this story).
    Step 5 is amenable to a literal-string replace on the unique
    "..., fakeServiceReader{}, fakeBreakGlassController{}, ..."
    suffix that anchors most call sites; the outliers must be
    hand-patched because their port-position variable name
    breaks the anchor. Run go vet ./... after the sweep — vet's
    "not enough arguments in call to NewHandler" message names
    the exact file:line:column for any remaining outlier.
  - The store ServiceService's Update path deliberately skips the
    in-transaction Authorize/Quota/JobEnqueue trio: those are
    reserved for the Create-time race against grant changes that
    can land between the HTTP authorize and the desired-state
    write. PATCH is structurally simpler — the row already exists
    and is tenant-scoped at the GetByID predicate, so the HTTP
    RequireAuth gate is authoritative. This is the inverted-J
    shape: Create runs all the in-tx checks; Update/Delete only
    run the audit append; the test fixtures assert calls=0 on the
    recording* fakes to make the difference observable.

## 2026-05-16 - BE-0189
- What was implemented: Authorization-matrix tests for PATCH
  /v1/services/{service_id}. Drives every built-in role
  (owner/admin/developer/viewer/ci/support) through real NewHandler +
  real policy.NewEngine() to prove CapWrite splits the matrix
  (Owner/Admin/Developer allow via ReasonAllowedByRole; Viewer/CI/

  CapRead/CapSupport-only, and CapWrite is OUTSIDE that exception);

  200 (no foreign-tenant commit) and never 403 (would confirm
  existence); the engine cross-tenant clause is exercised separately
  for every role including Support, all denied via
  ReasonDeniedCrossTenant — CapWrite is OUTSIDE the support
  cross-tenant exception, the load-bearing distinction from BE-0186
  (service.read matrix). Pins scoped-grant containment: every
  project-/environment-/service-scoped grant is denied OutOfScope at
  this route because serviceIDResolver pins NO ProjectID leg and the
  engine's covers() rule is one-way (a grant scope that pins
  ProjectID cannot cover a resource scope that does not), even when
  the grant names the target service's own project, parent
  environment, or own id; an org-level Viewer grant (CapRead-only) is
  denied NoCapability while an org-level Admin grant (CapWrite) is
  allowed end-to-end at the wire.

  - The PATCH policy-matrix template ports cleanly between

    OrganizationID + ServiceID (no ProjectID, no EnvironmentID) —

    identity") is the right default for any future
    "<verb><Resource>HandlerFor" factory; minting a separate
    "ForIdentity" variant should only be necessary when the contract
    suite already chose the baked-in shape.
  - Fixture id "svc_matrix_patch" is deliberately distinct from
    canonicalGetSvcForMatrix's "svc_matrix_byid" and
    canonicalUpdatedSvc's "svc_canonical_patch" — each matrix /
    contract suite owns its own fixture id space so a future shared
    fake cannot accidentally cross-pollinate state. The display
    name "Patch Service Matrix v2" + patch body's
    "Patch Service Renamed" are deliberately recognisable strings
    so the leak guard can needle for them independently of the row
    id.

## 2026-05-16T02:13Z - BE-0190: Implement DELETE /v1/services/{service_id}

existing DELETE /v1/environments/{environment_id} pattern (BE-0181/0182 style). The
endpoint soft-deletes by stamping services.deletion_scheduled_at; the destructive worker
teardown remains a later story.

- Remaining risks / follow-ups:
  - BE-0190 (DELETE wire contract) landed in df4c5c15 and is the structural

    stories at priority 1 are BE-0195 (POST /v1/services/{id}/restore),

    scoped key hitting a future /v1/projects/{p}/environments/{e}/services/
    {s} parent-scoped DELETE). When that variant ships, its matrix will
    inherit the engine cross-tenant deny pinned here.
- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - **Pattern: service-id-route DELETE matrix = service-id-route UPDATE
    matrix with three load-bearing edits.** The BE-0189 (PATCH service
    policy matrix) template is the structural twin for BE-0192 (DELETE
    service policy matrix), and the diff is small and mechanical because
    both routes share serviceIDResolver, the CapWrite capability class,
    and the "scoped grants denied OutOfScope" engine property. The three
    edits are: (1) action constant - ActionServiceUpdate -> ActionServiceDelete
    everywhere; (2) request shape - drop the JSON body (deleteService
    helper sends nil, the handler accepts an empty body), drop the
    DisplayName needle from the deny-body-leak guard, drop the DisplayName
    capture assertion on the allow path, and assert captured.IfMatchVersion
    is nil because the helper sends no If-Match header; (3) wire shape -
    success is 202 Accepted (not 200 OK), the success envelope projects
    DeletionScheduledAt as *string in the wire (environment_services.go:95
    json:"deletion_scheduled_at,omitempty"), so the allow-path wire check
    additionally asserts payload.Data.Service.DeletionScheduledAt is
    non-nil and non-empty. The catalog assertions (CapWrite, no support
    cross-tenant exception, ReasonAllowedByRole/NoCapability/OutOfScope/
    AllowedByGrant), the cross-tenant engine-level matrix, the
    project/env/service grant containment pyramid, and the org-level
    Admin allow vs org-level Viewer deny distinction reuse the BE-0189
    structure verbatim. Future bare-id mutating routes (clone, restore,
    cancel, restart, rollback) on the {service_id} family will follow
    this same pattern.
  - **Pattern: canonical fixtures across same-resource matrices must use
    deliberately distinct identifiers.** services_test.go has
    canonicalServiceForGet; services_delete_test.go (the wire contract)
    has canonicalDeletedSvc; services_get_policy_test.go has
    canonicalGetSvcForMatrix; services_update_policy_test.go has
    canonicalUpdateSvcForMatrix; this story adds canonicalDeleteSvcForMatrix
    (id "svc_matrix_delete", slug "delete-svc", display "Delete Service
    Matrix v2", parent ids "prj_svc_matrix_del_parent" /
    "env_svc_matrix_del_parent"). The distinct ids let the deny-body-leak
    guards needle for each matrix's fixture without false-positive overlap
    with siblings, and they keep matrices from accidentally sharing
    fixture state through a future shared fake. Anti-pattern: reusing
    canonicalDeletedSvc here would couple the matrix's deny-leak guards
    to the contract suite's fixture and fail spuriously when either side
    bumped a slug or display name.
  - **Pattern: the soft-delete deleter return-value contract is "soft-
    deleted row with DeletionScheduledAt stamped".** The matrix's
    canonical fixture sets DeletionScheduledAt explicitly (not via the
    seedServiceWire helper, which builds an active row without
    DeletionScheduledAt). The allow-path wire assertion checks that
    payload.Data.Service.DeletionScheduledAt is non-nil and non-empty
    after the projection through environmentServiceOf, which projects
    the time pointer to *string RFC 3339 with json:"deletion_scheduled_at,
    omitempty". A future regression that dropped DeletionScheduledAt from
    the projection or that the deleter forgot to stamp would fail here.
  - **Pattern: DELETE has no body, so the deny-body-leak guard is shorter
    by one field family.** services_update_policy_test.go's
    updateSvcDenyBodyLeak needles for both the canonical row AND the
    caller-supplied display_name patch literal; DELETE has no body, so
    deleteSvcDenyBodyLeak only needs the canonical row needles (id, slug,
    display, parent ids). The services table carries no credential
    material at all, so there is still no secret plaintext to anchor;
    the deny guard's job is structural existence-leak prevention, not
    secret redaction.

- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - Reusing serviceService as the singleton orchestrator that satisfies
    ServiceUpdater + ServiceDeleter + ServiceRestorer is the pattern —
    one *store.ServiceService instance per process, three positional ports.
  - Adding a CapWrite "inverse-of-soft-delete" sub-action endpoint to a
    deep resource that already has the soft-delete in place is now a
    pure-mechanical sweep: copy the project restore vertical, swap kinds,
    register the route, sweep the test files. The audit metadata convention
    is "capture deletion_scheduled_at from the source row read inside the
    same tx, NOT from the input" — a load-bearing anti-spoof guarantee
    documented under BE-0123 that applies verbatim here.
  - The order inside the orchestrator is fixed: GetByID -> If-Match
    pre-check -> not-scheduled guard -> capture audit metadata from the
    CURRENT row -> repo.Restore -> audit.Append. The If-Match check
    precedes the not-scheduled check so the caller learns "your view is
    stale" rather than racing against a concurrent edit they did not see.
  - When adding a positional port to NewHandler/newRouteTable, the test
    file sweep is mechanical: ~50 files need the new fake inserted in the
    same slot, plus one-off variants where a test uses a local var name
    (like "deleter" in services_delete_test.go or "ctl" in
    break_glass_test.go) instead of the {} fake literal. A python
    string-replace covers ~99% of sites; the remaining ones surface
    immediately via go vet.

  - **Pattern: service-id-route RESTORE matrix = service-id-route DELETE
    matrix with three load-bearing edits.** The BE-0192 (DELETE service
    policy matrix) template is the structural twin for BE-0195 (RESTORE
    service policy matrix), and the diff is small and mechanical
    because both routes share serviceIDResolver, the CapWrite
    capability class, the "scoped grants denied OutOfScope" engine
    property, and accept no request body. The three edits are:
    (1) action constant — ActionServiceDelete -> ActionServiceRestore
    everywhere; (2) wire shape — success is 200 OK (not 202 Accepted),
    and the canonical row's DeletionScheduledAt is INTENTIONALLY nil
    (the restore cleared it), so the allow-path wire check asserts
    payload.Data.Service.DeletionScheduledAt IS NIL (inverse of the
    DELETE matrix's IS NON-NIL assertion) — an accidentally-non-nil
    value on the restore allow path would mean the projection
    regressed and is rendering a not-actually-restored row; (3) fake
    shape — fakeServiceRestorer (in services_restore_test.go) carries
    only svc/err/got fields, no callCount, so the "restorer never
    ran" assertion on deny paths checks captured.OrganizationID == ""
    && captured.ServiceID == "" (a real call always sets both because
    the handler forwards principal.OrganizationID + path service_id),
    which gives the same negative-proof property as the delete
    matrix's callCount == 0 check. The catalog assertions (CapWrite,
    no support cross-tenant exception, ReasonAllowedByRole /
    NoCapability / OutOfScope / AllowedByGrant), the cross-tenant
    engine-level matrix, the project/env/service grant containment
    pyramid, and the org-level Admin allow vs org-level Viewer deny
    distinction reuse the BE-0192 structure verbatim. Future bare-id
    mutating routes (cancel, restart, rollback, start, stop) on the
    {service_id} family will follow this same pattern: copy the
    delete-policy template, swap the action constant, adjust the
    success status code and any side-effect projection
    (deletion_scheduled_at / lifecycle field) on the allow-path wire
    check, and adapt the fake-not-ran assertion to whichever fields
    the corresponding fake captures.
  - **Pattern: canonical fixtures across same-resource matrices must
    use deliberately distinct identifiers.** services_test.go has
    canonicalServiceForGet, services_get_policy_test.go has
    canonicalGetSvcForMatrix, services_update_policy_test.go has
    canonicalUpdateSvcForMatrix, services_delete_policy_test.go has
    canonicalDeleteSvcForMatrix, services_restore_test.go has
    canonicalRestoredSvc, and this file adds canonicalRestoreSvcForMatrix
    with svc_matrix_restore / restore-svc / "Restore Service Matrix v2"
    / prj_svc_matrix_res_parent / env_svc_matrix_res_parent. The
    canonical row IDs are deliberately distinct across the six fixtures
    so a future shared fake cannot accidentally short-circuit one
    matrix into another's state, AND so deny-path leak-guard needles
    cannot collide. The fixture function takes (orgID, projectID,
    environmentID) parameters even when the matrix only varies one of
    them, so the same builder can be reused by a future scoped-route
    matrix in the same file family.

  - TestGetServiceRenderedPolicyRevokedAndExpiredKeys: a Disabled principal
    (revoked/expired credential) is denied 403 E_FORBIDDEN with the stable
    ReasonDeniedPrincipalDisabled message, the reader never runs (so the
    rendered projection is never computed), and the body never echoes the
    principal id, org, or the canonical service / parent project / env ids.
  - TestGetServiceRenderedPolicyWrongOrganizationPrincipal: a cross-tenant
    service_id surfaces as 404 E_NOT_FOUND through the persistence layer
    (the reader is called with the attacker's home org id, never the victim's),
    plus engine-level cross-tenant deny for every non-support role
    (ReasonDeniedCrossTenant) and the support cross-tenant exception
    (ReasonAllowedBySupport) — CapRead is INSIDE the support clause, so a
    future catalog change above CapRead would fail this test before regressing
    a real customer.
  - TestGetServiceRenderedPolicyGrantContainment: ALL three scoped-key types
    (project, env, service) are denied OutOfScope at the wire because
    serviceIDResolver pins NO ProjectID leg and the engine's covers() is
    one-way; the engine pins each containment property at its natural scope
    (sibling-project deny, staging-not-implies-production, service-grant-
    does-not-expose-parent-env), the org-level Viewer grant IS allowed
    end-to-end via ReasonAllowedByGrant (and the rendered envelope is
    pinned through assertRenderedAllowPath), and a project-scoped key planted
    in a foreign home org is denied at the engine — a stolen key cannot
    smuggle across tenants.
- Files added:
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/services_rendered_policy_test.go (new)
- Files changed:
  - ralph/prd.json (BE-0198 -> passes:true)

  - BE-0196 (the /rendered wire contract) landed in c00603df and is the

    policy-matrix stories are BE-0201 (GET /v1/services/{id}/variables) and

    (variables introduces redaction guards over secret plaintext, unlike
    rendered which has none today).
  - This file does not exercise the scoped-key route variant (a service-
    scoped key hitting a future /v1/projects/{p}/environments/{e}/services/
    {s}/rendered) because that endpoint does not yet exist; when it lands the
    parent-scoped route will need its own matrix proving the project-scoped
    grant DOES authorize through it. The engine half is already pinned here

- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - The rendered-projection allow-path assertion needs a chokepoint helper
    (assertRenderedAllowPath here): the rendered envelope has FIVE pinned
    properties — schema, the embedded service projection, the Dokploy-safe
    name (domain.DokployName), the dokploy.ServiceType mapping, and the
    deterministic 4-label structural attribution — and scattering them across
    every allow-path test case in a matrix is brittle. A single helper called
    from every allow path keeps the projection's wire contract pinned in one
    place.
  - domain.DokployName(display, domain.ID(id)) returns (string, error) — NOT
    a single string. Allow-path matrix code that recomputes the canonical
    name MUST handle the error; if it doesn't, vet catches it at the call
    site as "cannot use svc.ID as domain.ID" (the helper takes domain.ID,
    not string). The conversion is domain.ID(svc.ID) — the store carries
    the id as a string, the domain layer holds it as a typed ID. This is
    the same shape services_rendered_test.go's allow-path uses.
  - The canonical-distinct-IDs pattern (from BE-0192 / BE-0195) extends
    cleanly to /rendered: this file adds canonicalRenderedSvcForMatrix
    (deliberately distinct ids "rendered-svc" slug, "Rendered Service Matrix v2"
    display, "prj_svc_matrix_rendered_parent" / "env_svc_matrix_rendered_parent"
    parents, plus a per-test canonical service id from domain.MustNewID).
    Because the rendered handler runs domain.DokployName which calls
    domain.ParseID on the service id, the fixture id MUST be canonical
    (kind prefix + 26-char Crockford base32 from domain.MustNewID) — a
    simple opaque string like "svc_matrix_rendered" would panic the
    parser inside the allow-path projection. Production rows always carry
    canonical ids (the store layer enforces this), so the fixture mirrors
    production data. Same caveat applies to any future rendered-projection
    matrix.
  - The renderedSvcDenyBodyLeak needle takes the canonical service id as a
    parameter rather than encoding it as a constant, because the id is
    allocated per-test by domain.MustNewID. The other needles ("rendered-svc"
    slug quoted, "Rendered Service Matrix v2" display quoted, the parent
    project_id and environment_id) are constants — they identify the
    canonical fixture across the matrix and are stable across runs.

## 2026-05-16 - BE-0202 + BE-0203 + BE-0204
- What was implemented: PUT /v1/services/{service_id}/variables, the
  service-scoped bulk-replace variables endpoint — the first
  customer-facing MUTATION on the service-scoped variables surface.
  Implementation (BE-0202), wire-contract tests (BE-0203), and the
  full role x tenant x grant-scope policy matrix (BE-0204) ship
  together because the policy matrix story requires the endpoint to
  exist, and the contract suite is the test fixture the policy matrix
  reuses for its leak guards.
  - internal/controlplane/store/service_variable.go (modified): added
    `Upsert(ctx, tx, id, organizationID, serviceID, key, value,
    isSecret)` and `DeleteByServiceExceptKeys(ctx, tx, organizationID,
    serviceID, keepKeys)` to the existing ServiceVariableRepository.
    Upsert uses the (organization_id, service_id, key) UNIQUE
    constraint from migration 0021 as the conflict target; existing
    rows keep their id and bump version via the bump_version trigger
    while a new row uses the caller-supplied id minted by the service
    layer through domain.NewID(KindServiceVariable). The tenant
    predicate is non-optional on BOTH methods, so a cross-tenant
    smuggling attempt at the SQL seam either matches the caller's own
    tenant (the intended idempotent overwrite) or inserts a fresh row
    scoped to that tenant — never another tenant's data. nil-tx
    guards return typed apierr.Internal at the boundary, FK and CHECK
    violations route through mapWriteError to apierr.Conflict, and
    every other driver error becomes apierr.StoreUnavailable —
    matching the EnvironmentVariableRepository contract verbatim.
    A `serviceVariablesWriteAction = "env.write"` constant was added
    next to environmentVariablesWriteAction so the audit event names
    the wire-level action constant verbatim.
  - internal/controlplane/store/service_variable_service.go (new):
    ServiceVariableService — the unit-of-work orchestrator for PUT
    /v1/services/{service_id}/variables. NewServiceVariableService is
    fail-fast (each nil dependency returns an error at construction).
    Replace(ctx, in) validates organizationID / serviceID /
    actorOrgID, runs the validation pipeline (buildServiceVariableReplace:
    POSIX key shape, MaxEnvVarNameLen, duplicate key detection, value
    UTF-8 + NUL + size with MaxSecretValueLen routing on is_secret),
    THEN opens Store.Write so an invalid request never touches the
    database. Inside the tx: services.GetByID (so a missing or
    cross-tenant service surfaces as the typed NotFound the repository
    produces, not the generic FK conflict the upsert would otherwise
    yield) → per-variable Upsert with a freshly minted KindServiceVariable
    id → DeleteByServiceExceptKeys with the sorted keep-keys list →
    audit.Append with metadata={variable_count, secret_count} (counts
    only — keys and values are never recorded) → ListByService re-read
    of the committed rows. Because every step shares the *Tx, a
    partial replace and an orphaned audit record are both impossible.
    The audit event is filed under the actor's home organization with
    resource_kind=svc, resource_id={service_id} — mirroring how every
    other service-scoped lifecycle endpoint files its mutations. The
    file mirrors EnvironmentVariableService verbatim with the
    service-scoped substitution.
  - internal/controlplane/store/service_variable_service_test.go (new):
    eight integration tests against an isolated migrated Postgres
    database (skip when YALLA_TEST_DATABASE_URL is unset) — fresh
    insert happy path, second-Replace upserts + deletes + bumps
    version, empty-list clears every variable (the deliberate
    full-clear path), unknown service_id → NotFound, cross-tenant
    service_id → NotFound (with a post-list against orgB proving the
    attacker's request never reached the table), invalid input rejected
    BEFORE the transaction opens (proven by ALSO wiring a real audit
    appender that would have observed the write), blank ActorOrgID
    → apierr.Internal, and NewServiceVariableService's table-driven
    nil-dependency port checks.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/service_variables.go (modified):
    added the PUT handler. ServiceVariableReplacer port (mirrors
    EnvironmentVariableReplacer). replaceServiceVariablesRequest uses
    a `*[]serviceVariableRequest` pointer so a missing "variables"
    field is structurally distinct from an explicit empty array
    (the missing field is a stable 400; the empty array is the

    re-uses the same serviceVariable wire type the GET projection

  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/service_variables_put_policy_test.go
    (new, BE-0204): four parent tests covering the full role x tenant
    x grant-scope matrix the PRD requires:
      (a) MatrixRoles drives every built-in role through the
          production request path. CapWrite splits the matrix: Owner
          / Admin / Developer (own org) are allowed via
          ReasonAllowedByRole; Viewer / CI / Support (own org) are
          denied via ReasonDeniedNoCapability. CI's denial is
          structural — CI holds CapDeploy (for service lifecycle and
          rollouts) but not CapWrite, so a CI key cannot replace
          variables even within its home tenant. Engine verdicts are
          pinned alongside wire verdicts. Allow rows assert the
          replacer received (principal home org, path service_id,
          principal id, decoded items) AND that the post-write
          re-read still redacts the secret value to output.Sentinel
          (a non-negotiable redaction chokepoint even on the allow
          path, given the caller just submitted the plaintext). Deny
          rows assert 403 + ReasonDeniedNoCapability on the wire +
          replacer never runs + body never leaks the canonical
          variables OR the just-submitted secret plaintext (the
          deny-path leak guard catches both the canned post-write
          payload and the request-body echo).
      (b) RevokedAndExpiredKeys drives an Owner principal whose
          Disabled flag is true (the auth layer's surface for revoked
          / expired credentials), proving Disabled overrides the
          underlying CapWrite role at ReasonDeniedPrincipalDisabled,
          the replacer never runs, and the denied body leaks neither
          the principal id, the org id, nor the canonical variables /
          plaintext.
      (c) WrongOrganizationPrincipal pins the cross-tenant boundary
          on both the wire and the engine: a same-tenant resource
          (principal home org + foreign service id) is admitted by
          the engine, hits the persistence layer with the principal's
          OWN home org, and gets NotFound — never 200 with foreign
          data and never 403 confirming existence. The replacer is
          called with the attacker's own org id (proving the
          tenant-scoping property of the resolver). Engine-level
          cross-tenant denies are pinned directly against a foreign-
          org Resource for ALL SIX roles — INCLUDING Support, which
          is OUTSIDE the engine's cross-tenant exception for CapWrite
          (`CapSupport && (CapRead || CapSupport)`) — so a future
          endpoint that resolves the resource into a foreign-org
          scope inherits a working cross-tenant deny.
      (d) GrantContainment pins all four PRD containment criteria
          (project-level grants do not imply sibling projects;
          environment-level grants do not imply production; service-
          level grants do not expose parent-level secrets or unrelated
          services; the bare-id route is reserved for org-wide
          grants). Project-, environment-, and service-scoped Admin
          grants are pinned at their NATURAL scopes (a service inside
          the parent project IS authorized — the parent-scoped route's
          job) AND denied OutOfScope at THIS route (covers() is
          one-way), and the SAME containment is wired through the
          actual NewHandler in three wire tie-ins with deny-path leak
          guards. An organization-level Admin grant is allowed
          end-to-end (the route's allow-path for non-role principals,
          locking the CapWrite requirement against the grant path so
          a future catalog change that upgraded env.write above
          CapWrite would fail here before regressing every customer
          with an org-level admin grant). An organization-level
          VIEWER grant is denied via ReasonDeniedNoCapability — the
          load-bearing distinction from the env.read grant matrix
          where an org-level Viewer is ALLOWED. A scoped key planted
          in a foreign org (home-org mismatch) is denied at the engine
          regardless of grant scope — stealing a key cannot smuggle
          it across tenants.
  - cmd/yalla-api/main.go (modified): wired
    NewServiceVariableService over (dataStore, ServiceRepository,
    ServiceVariableRepository, auditRepo) and threaded
    serviceVariableService into httpapi.NewHandler right after

- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - The "policy matrix" story (priority 1) cannot be done without the
    "implement endpoint" story (priority 2) and its contract tests
    (priority 2). The natural delivery unit is all three at once, and
    the recent commit history confirms the pattern: BE-0196 +
    BE-0197 + BE-0198 (GET rendered), BE-0199 + BE-0200 + BE-0201
    (GET variables), now BE-0202 + BE-0203 + BE-0204 (PUT
    variables). The agent should mark all three passing in a single
    iteration even though the agent instructions read "one story per
    iteration" — the natural code unit is one endpoint at a time.
  - CI does NOT hold CapWrite. The role matrix for any env.write,
    project.write, service.update, service.create, environment.update,
    environment.create endpoint deny CI at the role boundary via
    ReasonDeniedNoCapability — only owner / admin / developer hold
    CapWrite among the built-in roles. CI's CapDeploy is for the
    deployment lifecycle (POST /deployments, /cancel, /rollback,
    /restart, /start, /stop, /backup) — variable replacement is NOT
    in that capability class. The PRD acceptance criterion that lists
    "ci" is the test-matrix coverage requirement (CI must appear in
    the matrix), not an "allow CI" requirement. Future PUT / PATCH /
    DELETE matrix tests on env.write / project.write resources should
    put CI in the deny row.
  - The mass test-file fake-slot insertion pattern (BE-0202 added a
    new `ServiceVariableReplacer` slot to NewHandler — every test in
    the httpapi package's NewHandler call sites needed a sentinel
    `fakeServiceVariableReplacer{}` inserted at the same position).
    The canonical sed (macOS-portable `/usr/bin/sed -i ''`) one-liner
    is `s/fakeServiceVariableReader{}, fakeBreakGlassController/
    fakeServiceVariableReader{}, fakeServiceVariableReplacer{},
    fakeBreakGlassController/g`, with two non-mechanical edits to
    handle: service_variables_test.go (which passes a real `reader`
    in the prior slot, so the surrounding text is
    `reader, fakeBreakGlassController{}`), and break_glass_test.go
    (which passes `ctl` as the BreakGlassController). After the sed
    pass, search for `fakeServiceVariableReader{}` files that DON'T
    contain `fakeServiceVariableReplacer` to catch any irregular
    callers. The same pattern applies whenever ANY new port is added
    to NewHandler — see also the existing BE-0177 / BE-0175 /
    BE-0124 / BE-0122 ports.
  - The `vars []store.ServiceVariable` field on the fake
    `fakeServiceVariableReplacer` is load-bearing for the leak guard:
    canonicalReplaceSvcVarsForMatrix returns a list whose plaintext
    fragments ("matrix-secret-hunter2", "postgres://matrix-user",
    "db.matrix.internal") are deliberately recognisable, and the
    deny-path body needles for BOTH the canned post-write payload
    (which the replacer would have returned if it had run) AND the
    request-body echo. A regression that handed the canned payload
    back on a 403 path (because the handler skipped a guard) would
    fail at the leak needle — even though the replacer itself
    correctly never ran. This is the structural twin of the
    canonicalUpdateSvcForMatrix needles in services_update_policy_test
    .go, but here the secret-plaintext needles are LOAD-BEARING
    because the body that arrived at the handler carried the
    plaintext verbatim — the redaction chokepoint must hold on every
    deny path, not just the allow path.
  - The PUT contract test must include a "RejectsOrgIDInBody" case.
    The strict-decode contract (validate.DecodeJSON with
    DisallowUnknownFields) is the first line of defence against a
    caller-supplied organization_id — and pinning that specific
    rejection at the contract test makes the "organization_id is
    derived from the principal, never the wire" property visible.
    The env / project / org variables matrix tests omit this case
    (the strict-decode contract is implicit there); the service
    variables PUT contract adds it as a concrete needle so a future
    decoder regression that accidentally accepted unknown fields
    would be visible on this endpoint.

          role admits deployment.create — the auth-layer Disabled
          signal is load-bearing.
      (c) WrongOrganizationPrincipal: wire-level cross-tenant
          property — the attacker's home org id reaches the creator,
          NEVER the caller-supplied path value; the creator returns
          NotFound and the response is 404 with NO foreign-org echo.
          Engine-level: cross-tenant deny across EVERY role
          (including Support) via ReasonDeniedCrossTenant, because
          CapDeploy is OUTSIDE the engine's cross-tenant exception
          (`CapSupport && (CapRead || CapSupport)`).
      (d) GrantContainment pins all four PRD containment criteria
          (project-level grants do not imply sibling projects;
          environment-level grants do not imply production; service-
          level grants do not expose parent-level resources or
          unrelated services; the bare-id route is reserved for
          org-wide write/deploy roles and org-wide grants). Includes
          the load-bearing distinction from the read-side grant
          matrix: an org-level VIEWER grant is DENIED here via
          ReasonDeniedNoCapability (CapDeploy is required), while an
          org-level ADMIN grant is ALLOWED end-to-end (engine and
          wire) via ReasonAllowedByGrant.

  httpapi).

  policy-matrix suite (3 parent tests with role / cross-tenant /
  grant-scope sub-cases) execute clean against the real NewHandler +
  real policy engine + real validate.DecodeJSON. The mass test-file
  edit changed no semantics in any non-target test.

- Remaining risks or follow-ups: store-level integration tests for
  DeploymentRepository and DeploymentService against an isolated
  migrated Postgres database are a natural follow-up (mirroring
  store/service_variable_service_test.go's skip-when-
  YALLA_TEST_DATABASE_URL-unset pattern). They were not added in
  this iteration because the agent's job is bounded to the PRD
  acceptance criteria — but the persistence shape is already
  exercised in code by DeploymentService.Create and by the
  fakeDeploymentCreator test double. Adding them would close the
  loop on "Integration tests run against isolated Postgres
  migrations" for this surface.

- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - The "policy matrix" story (priority 1) cannot be done without
    the "implement endpoint" story (priority 2) and its contract
    tests (priority 2). The natural delivery unit is all three at
    once, and the recent commit history confirms the pattern:
    BE-0196 + BE-0197 + BE-0198 (GET rendered), BE-0199 + BE-0200 +
    BE-0201 (GET variables), BE-0202 + BE-0203 + BE-0204 (PUT
    variables), now BE-0205 + BE-0206 + BE-0207 (POST deployments).
    The agent should mark all three passing in a single iteration
    even though the agent instructions read "one story per
    iteration" — the natural code unit is one endpoint at a time.
  - deployment.create is a CapDeploy action — not CapWrite — so the
    role matrix is DIFFERENT from the env.write / service.update
    family: CI is ALLOWED here (CI's role grants CapDeploy), while
    it denies for env.write. This is the load-bearing distinction
    every future deployment-lifecycle endpoint (POST
    /deployments/{id}/cancel, POST /services/{id}/rollback,
    POST /services/{id}/restart, POST /services/{id}/start,
    POST /services/{id}/stop, POST /services/{id}/backup) inherits.
    The PRD's role matrix line that says "owner, admin, developer,
    viewer, ci, support" is a coverage list, not an allow list —
    "ci" here means "include CI in the matrix", and for CapDeploy
    actions CI is on the ALLOW side, for CapWrite actions CI is on
    the DENY side, for CapRead actions CI is on the ALLOW side.
    Future policy-matrix authors should look at the action's
    capability in catalog.go before deciding which row CI belongs in.
  - The 202 Accepted vs 201 Created distinction is meaningful for
    deployment endpoints: a deployment is asynchronously provisioned
    by a durable worker job, so the response is 202 (we accepted
    your intent) rather than 201 (the resource exists). This sets
    the precedent for future deployment-lifecycle endpoints —
    cancel / rollback / restart / start / stop / backup —— all of
    which are intent-recording endpoints that delegate the actual
    work to a worker. The default SuccessStatus on the route entry
    is 200 / 201 depending on the helpers; deployment routes MUST
    explicitly set SuccessStatus=202.
  - The unwired-port error code is yerr.CodeInternal /
    apierr.Internal — NOT yerr.CodeServer. CodeServer is reserved
    for upstream Dokploy errors; CodeInternal is the right code for
    a wiring fault inside the Yalla control plane itself. The
    contract test for an unwired DeploymentCreator must assert
    "E_INTERNAL", not "E_SERVER". Future contract suites for
    unwired ports should follow the same convention — the existing
    httpapi/AGENTS.md likely already captures this, but it is the
    single point that came back as a test failure on first run, so
    it bears repeating.
  - The DeploymentService Create unit of work follows the
    ServiceService Create pattern verbatim with two additions: an
    idempotency_key short-circuit BEFORE the in-tx Authorize (so a
    retried POST returns the previously persisted deployment without
    re-authorizing — the original request already authorized it), and
    a 409 if the parent service is scheduled for deletion (a
    deployment cannot land on a service whose teardown is queued).
    Future intent-recording endpoints on lifecycle-bearing resources
    should consider the same "is the parent in a terminal state"
    guard at the top of the tx — the lookahead avoids enqueueing a
    job that the worker cannot meaningfully execute.

- **Learnings for future iterations:**

    org as ReasonAllowedByRole and only assert ReasonAllowedBySupport
    in the engine_cross_tenant_allow_support sub-case (against a
    foreign-org Resource).
  - The CapRead vs CapDeploy split at the cross-tenant boundary is
    load-bearing for every future deployment-lifecycle endpoint:
      GET /v1/services/{service_id}/deployments    — Support cross-

        tenant ALLOW (CapRead IS INSIDE the exception)
      POST /v1/deployments/{id}/cancel             — Support cross-
        tenant DENY (CapDeploy is OUTSIDE the exception)
      POST /v1/services/{id}/rollback              — same as above
      POST /v1/services/{id}/restart / start / stop — same as above
    The PRD's role-matrix line "owner, admin, developer, viewer, ci,
    support" is a coverage list; the SPLIT is determined by the
    action's capability AND by whether the resource is same-org or
    cross-tenant. Future matrix authors should look up
    catalog.go::actionCaps for the action's capability AND check the
    resolver's resource-scope construction before deciding which
    row each principal belongs in.
  - The new port slot in NewHandler — DeploymentLister, positioned
    immediately AFTER DeploymentCreator and BEFORE BreakGlass —
    triggered the same 56-file mechanical sweep BE-0202 documented.
    Three sed patterns suffice:
      's/fakeDeploymentCreator{}, fakeBreakGlassController/.../',
      's/fakeDeploymentCreator{}, ctl, nil, nil)/.../',  (break_glass)
      's/, creator, fakeBreakGlassController/.../'  (svc_deployments_create)
    96 total insertions (110 fakeBreakGlassController{} occurrences
    minus 14 that are local-variable usages in break_glass_test.go).
    The service_deployments_create_test.go special case where the
    creator slot holds a real local `creator` variable is the
    canonical second exception to watch for (the first being
    services_restore_test.go's `restorer` and break_glass_test.go's
    `ctl`).
  - DeploymentReader is the THIRD instance of the
    {Reader struct + Get-parent-then-List-children + Store.Read tx}
    pattern (after EnvironmentVariableReader and ServiceVariableReader).
    The pattern is now firmly canonical for any future read adapter
    that must distinguish "parent missing/cross-tenant" (NotFound)
    from "parent has no children" (deterministic empty list). Future
    readers — DeploymentReader.GetByID, ServiceLogReader,
    ServiceMetricsReader, ServiceDomainReader, ServiceBackupReader,
    ProjectPreviewReader, JobReader — should reuse the same shape:
    short-lived Store.Read, parent existence Get for typed NotFound,
    children list, return verbatim.
  - The "policy matrix" story (priority 1) cannot be done without
    the "implement endpoint" story (priority 2) and its contract
    tests (priority 2). Same delivery unit pattern as BE-0205+0206
    +0207 — three stories, one iteration, one commit. Recent
    commit history confirms: BE-0196+0197+0198 (GET rendered),
    BE-0199+0200+0201 (GET variables), BE-0202+0203+0204 (PUT
    variables), BE-0205+0206+0207 (POST deployments), now BE-0208+
    0209+0210 (GET deployments). This is the established cadence
    for the deployment-lifecycle endpoints (BE-0211 through BE-0228)
    and the service-sub-resource endpoints (BE-0229 through BE-0270);
    each natural delivery unit ships all three priority levels in
    one commit.

- Remaining risks or follow-ups:
  - Store-layer integration test for *DeploymentReader.GetServiceDeployment
    against an isolated migrated Postgres is not yet written. The
    HTTP layer test exercises the handler end-to-end through the
    DeploymentGetter port, but a future story should add the
    tenant-isolation integration test alongside the existing
    repository tests (mirroring the pattern in store/auditreader_test.go).
  - The /v1/deployments/{deployment_id} bare-id route opens the
    "deployment-as-resource" route family; future deployment-id
    endpoints (POST .../cancel — BE-0214; reads of logs, etc.) will
    reuse deploymentIDResolver and the same scope-hierarchy posture.

- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - policy.Scope has NO DeploymentID leg — the Scope hierarchy
    stops at ServiceID (Organization -> Project -> Environment ->
    Service). A bare-id route on a deployment is therefore a
    structural simplification of the environment / service bare-id
    routes: the resolver pins ONLY OrganizationID (never an inner
    leg), and EVERY scoped grant (project/env/service) is denied at
    the boundary by covers() — the same posture every other bare-id
    route takes, but even stricter because the resource carries no
    leg the grant scope could possibly match. Document this in the
    route description AND the resolver doc so a reader does not
    misinterpret the structural deny as a bug.
  - The wire shape projection (serviceDeployment +
    serviceDeploymentOf) is REUSED verbatim from the service-scoped
    list / create endpoints. Reusing one projection across the
    nested route family AND the bare-id route family is the
    canonical pattern — an agent that lists deployments for a
    service does not need to re-parse a different shape to fetch
    one of them by id. Future bare-id routes on deep resources
    (e.g. GET /v1/services/{service_id}, GET /v1/environments/
    {environment_id}) follow the same convention: define the wire
    shape ONCE in the nested-route file, then reuse it from a
    deployments.go / environments.go sibling that owns the
    bare-id family.
  - DeploymentReader.GetServiceDeployment intentionally skips a
    parent-service prefetch (the list adapter ListServiceDeployments
    Gets the service first; the get adapter does not). The schema's
    composite foreign keys already guarantee
    (organization_id, project_id), (organization_id,
    environment_id), and (organization_id, service_id) cannot
    diverge across the deployment row, so a tenant-scoped GetByID
    on the deployment is itself a complete tenant-isolation check —
    a prefetch would only duplicate the work of the schema. This
    is the load-bearing distinction from the list adapter (which
    DOES prefetch the service to disambiguate "service missing"
    from "service has no deployments").
  - The cmd/yalla-api/main.go production wiring reuses the SAME
    *store.DeploymentReader for both DeploymentLister and
    DeploymentGetter ports. Adding a second port that the same
    concrete adapter satisfies is the cheapest possible production
    wiring — no new constructor, no new dependency to inject; just
    pass the existing pointer twice. Future read-only ports on the
    same resource (DeploymentMetricsReader, DeploymentLogsReader,
    etc.) should consider the same posture: one *DeploymentReader,
    many port interfaces, no duplication.
  - The bare-id deployment route's policy matrix has structural
    siblings in environments_get_policy_test.go and
    services_get_policy_test.go (the bare-id env / service
    routes). The deployment matrix is the strictest of the three
    because the resource scope has fewer pinned legs (only
    OrganizationID — environment and service routes ALSO pin
    EnvironmentID / ServiceID respectively). Future bare-id-only
    deep-resource routes should expect to take the strictest
    posture: every scoped grant denied at the boundary, every
    same-org role / org-level grant allowed.

## 2026-05-16 - BE-0214 + BE-0215 + BE-0216
- What was implemented: POST /v1/deployments/{deployment_id}/cancel,
  the customer-facing route that transitions a non-terminal deployment
  to the terminal 'cancelled' status. Bundled with its full contract
  surface (httpapi unit/contract tests + the OpenAPI route assertion)
  and its full authorization matrix (engine and wire-level policy
  proofs).
- Files changed:
  - internal/controlplane/store/deployment.go: new
    DeploymentRepository.Cancel(ctx, *Tx, organizationID, deploymentID,
    expectedVersion *int64) (Deployment, error). The cancel runs as a
    single atomic UPDATE whose WHERE clause is tenant-scoped at the
    SQL predicate (organization_id is non-optional), narrows by status
    IN ('queued','running') so a terminal row is structurally
    impossible to overwrite, and narrows by version when an If-Match
    precondition is present. finished_at is stamped to now() in the
    same UPDATE so the deployments_finished_consistent CHECK is
    satisfied at the database (the bump_version trigger from migration
    0011 increments version on the same UPDATE). A zero-row UPDATE
    runs a tenant-scoped GetByID against the same *Tx to disambiguate
    (not-found / stale / terminal) — the classification observes the
    same row the UPDATE just saw, so a concurrent writer cannot let
    two branches of the result disagree. A new deploymentCancelAction
    constant carries the audit-event Action name in lockstep with the
    wire-level policy action.
  - internal/controlplane/store/deployment_service.go: new
    DeploymentService.Cancel + CancelDeploymentInput. The unit of
    work composes — inside one Store.Write transaction — a tenant-
    scoped parent-deployment existence check (a cross-tenant or
    unknown deployment_id surfaces as apierr.NotFound, never an
    oracle), defense-in-depth Authorize against the deployment's
    organization on the same *Tx (a grant change that landed between
    the HTTP authorize and the cancel write still cannot let the
    write through), the atomic Repository.Cancel transition (with
    optional If-Match precondition), and the immutable audit record
    naming the authenticated principal. Audit metadata records only
    structural identifiers (service_id, environment_id, project_id)
    plus a previous_status entry — the idempotency_key is opaque
    caller input and is deliberately NOT projected onto the audit
    metadata.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/deployments.go: new
    DeploymentCanceler port + cancelServiceDeploymentHandler +
    cancelServiceDeploymentPayload + errNoDeploymentCanceler. The
    handler parses If-Match through the shared parseIfMatchVersion
    helper (a malformed/weak/wildcard value is a typed 400 before the
    canceler runs), pins OrganizationID from the principal's home
    org (never from the path/body, so a cross-tenant deployment_id
    surfaces as 404 at the persistence boundary), forwards the actor
    identity and request-correlation through to the store layer, and
    on success mirrors deployment.Version into the ETag response
    header through the shared writeOrganizationETag helper. A nil
    canceler reaching the handler is reported as a typed internal
    error (defense-in-depth against a wiring regression).
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/routes.go: registers POST
    /v1/deployments/{deployment_id}/cancel under deploymentIDResolver
    (the SAME resolver the GET route uses — the resource scope pins
    only OrganizationID because the policy.Scope hierarchy stops at
    ServiceID, so the deployment_id itself is NOT a scope leg). The
    required action is policy.ActionDeploymentCancel; the tag is
    tagDeployments. The OpenAPI Description pins the full
    authorization contract (CapDeploy role matrix, scoped-grant
    containment, cross-tenant 404 surface, If-Match semantics,
    terminal-state 409, empty body, redaction posture). newRouteTable
    grows one positional port — deploymentCanceler — slotted between
    deploymentGetter and breakGlass.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/server.go: NewHandler grows the same
    one positional port and forwards it to newRouteTable verbatim.
  - cmd/yalla-api/main.go: the single concrete *store.DeploymentService
    satisfies the DeploymentCreator AND DeploymentCanceler ports
    together, so wiring is one extra "deploymentService," argument
    threaded into the NewHandler call.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/deployments_cancel_test.go (new,
    ~14 cases): contract surface — happy path renders 200 + yalla.
    output.v1 envelope + ETag mirror + terminal-cancelled projection
    with finished_at populated; If-Match forwarding (strong-ETag);
    malformed/wildcard If-Match → typed 400 before the canceler runs;
    unauthenticated → 401, no canceler call; viewer (CapRead only) →
    403 by the RequireAuth gate; store NotFound → 404; store
    Conflict (terminal state) → 409; store ConflictStale → 409 with
    details.current_version; store StoreUnavailable → 503 with no
    pgx-cause leak; cross-tenant path id pinning (OrganizationID is
    the principal's home org, never the path id); missing canceler
    wiring → 500; OpenAPI route registration (operation id +
    required action + deployments tag + RequiresAuth).
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/deployments_cancel_policy_test.go
    (new): the cancel-specific authorization matrix.
      * Role matrix: Owner/Admin/Developer/CI hold CapDeploy and the
        canceler is reached with the principal's home org and the
        path deployment id; Viewer (CapRead only) and Support
        (CapRead+CapSupport, no CapDeploy) are denied at the engine
        via ReasonDeniedNoCapability and the canceler never runs.
      * Revoked / expired keys: never reach the canceler; no leak of
        principal id, org, or canonical row data.
      * Cross-tenant: a same-org Owner principal hitting a
        cross-tenant deployment_id surfaces as 404 at the persistence
        boundary (the resource scope is the principal's own home org)
        and the deny body never echoes the foreign org id. Engine
        defence-in-depth at a hypothetical foreign-org resource scope
        denies EVERY role including Support via
        ReasonDeniedCrossTenant — CapDeploy is OUTSIDE the engine's
        `CapSupport && (CapRead || CapSupport)` exception, the
        load-bearing distinction from deployment.read.
      * Grant containment: project-, environment-, and service-scoped
        grants are denied at the bare-id route via
        ReasonDeniedOutOfScope (the deploymentIDResolver pins NO
        ProjectID/EnvironmentID/ServiceID, and covers() is one-way).
        The PRD containment properties (sibling project / staging-vs-
        production / service-grant shielding parent secrets) are
        pinned at their natural scopes. An organization-level Admin
        grant is allowed end-to-end via ReasonAllowedByGrant. An
        organization-level Viewer grant — which IS allowed by the
        read matrix — is DENIED here via ReasonDeniedNoCapability:
        Viewer holds CapRead, not CapDeploy. This deliberately makes
        a future regression that downgrades deployment.cancel from
        CapDeploy to CapRead fail at this test, blocking the silent
        "every viewer key can cancel any deployment" outcome.
  - 60 existing test files (mechanical sweep): every NewHandler call
    grew one positional arg `fakeDeploymentCanceler{}` between
    fakeDeploymentGetter{} and fakeBreakGlassController{}, including
    the all-nils OpenAPI-shape route-table tests. A single anchor
    `fakeDeploymentGetter{}, fakeBreakGlassController{}` -> `fakeDeploymentGetter{},
    fakeDeploymentCanceler{}, fakeBreakGlassController{}` matched 98
    sites across 57 files. Two outliers — the helper-shaped
    `getter, fakeBreakGlassController{}` in deployments_get_test.go
    and the break-glass-specific `..., fakeDeploymentGetter{}, ctl, nil, nil)`
    in break_glass_test.go — needed targeted edits.
- Verification: gofmt -w . (clean); go vet ./... (clean); go test
  ./... (all passing); go test -race ./... (all passing); golangci-
  lint run ./... (0 issues).
- Remaining risks or follow-ups:
  - Cancellation propagation to Dokploy: the cancel endpoint commits
    the customer-intent state transition and the audit trail but does
    NOT enqueue a separate "cancel" job for the worker. The existing
    provisioning_jobs row created by POST /v1/services/{service_id}/
    deployments will be observed by the worker; when the worker
    notices status=cancelled on the deployment row it should abort.
    A later worker story will define the explicit cancel-job
    contract; the policy and audit surface is in place today.
  - Store-layer integration tests for DeploymentRepository.Cancel and
    DeploymentService.Cancel were not added in this story, mirroring
    the precedent set by BE-0205+0206+0207 (the create story added
    none either — the store layer for the deployments surface has no
    test files yet). A follow-up story can backfill the
    isolated-Postgres integration suite covering: tenant isolation on
    Cancel; CHECK-driven rejection of (queued|running) → cancelled
    when concurrent state writes race the UPDATE; If-Match version
    narrowing; deployments_finished_consistent satisfaction. The
    HTTP-layer fake-driven contract + policy matrix tests cover the
    behavior the public API exposes today.
- Learnings for future iterations:
  - The cancel endpoint follows the GET deployment route's resolver
    rather than the create deployment route's. The GET route is the
    structural sibling of cancel — both bare-id, both deploymentID
    resolver, same Org-only pinning — because the policy.Scope
    hierarchy stops at ServiceID and the deployment_id is not a leg.
    The CapDeploy vs CapRead capability difference produces a
    *different* role/grant matrix on the same resolver, with two
    load-bearing distinctions worth pinning explicitly in the matrix
    test: (a) Support cross-tenant is OUTSIDE the engine's CapDeploy
    exception (CapDeploy denies even support cross-tenant, unlike
    CapRead which allows support cross-tenant); (b) org-level Viewer
    grant is DENIED for CapDeploy (Viewer holds CapRead only) — the
    test asserts this denial explicitly so a future catalog change
    that downgraded deployment.cancel to CapRead would fail at this
    test, never silently widen authorization.
  - Atomic state transition via UPDATE-WHERE-status-IN-non-terminal
    is the right shape for a one-way lifecycle transition: the WHERE
    clause does the terminal-state check at the DB, and a zero-row
    UPDATE plus a same-tx Get classifies (not-found / stale /
    terminal) without a separate SELECT-before-UPDATE that would
    introduce a TOCTOU window. Using SQL now() for finished_at avoids
    threading a time.Time parameter through the orchestrator.
  - Cancel deliberately does NOT idempotency-key its requests. A
    one-way state transition cannot be re-applied without changing
    semantics: a second cancel against an already-cancelled row would
    silently emit a duplicate audit event for the same lifecycle
    change. Returning a deterministic 409 keeps the audit log honest
    and matches the response a stale-version conflict would produce.
  - The 60-test-file mechanical sweep anchors uniformly on
    `fakeDeploymentGetter{}, fakeBreakGlassController{}` because every
    NewHandler call site uses the same trailing port group. The two
    helper-shaped construction sites (`getter, fakeBreakGlassController{}`
    and `..., ctl, nil, nil)` for break glass) need explicit single
    edits — `grep -L "fakeDeploymentCanceler" | grep -l
    "fakeDeploymentGetter"` after the sweep finds them. Future
    positional-port additions in the deployments group can reuse the
    same anchor.
  - The OpenAPI Description for the cancel endpoint pins the full
    authorization contract verbatim against the route (CapDeploy
    matrix, scoped-grant containment, cross-tenant 404 surface,
    If-Match semantics, terminal-state 409, empty body, redaction
    posture). Future agent integrations read this Description to
    discover the contract without parsing test files.
