- Learnings for future iterations:
  - When a new quota dimension's owning service does NOT already
    have a quota port, the minimum atomic delivery grows from "one
    new test file" (BE-0331..BE-0336 sibling shape) to four
    coordinated change axes — see the Codebase Patterns entry for
    BE-0337. BE-0338 members is the next clone target; the
    MembershipService constructor likewise predates QuotaReserver,
    so the same four-axis delivery applies. BE-0339..0342 variable
    stories are NOT quota-dimension stories at all and use a
    different template.
  - The sealing-trap in quota_internal_test.go::TestQuotaResourceValid
    (`len(valid) == len(quotaResources)`) is the single test that
    catches a forgotten constant + membership-set entry pair in ONE
    failing line; the rest of the unit suite cannot, because Valid()
    only checks the map, never the constant set. Future quota
    dimension stories should expect this test to fail on the first
    `go test` and learn that the contract is "every QuotaResource
    constant MUST be in the membership set MUST be in the valid
    slice". The three things move together.
  - Pre-flight checking with `git stash` validates whether broad
    store-suite failures are pre-existing or introduced by the
    current change. The procedure is: stash tracked changes, move
    untracked new files to /tmp, run the failing test set, capture
    the failure-name set into /tmp/head_failures.txt, restore
    everything, re-run, diff. If the test-name sets are identical
    (only durations differ), the failures are pre-existing and
    out-of-scope. BE-0337 used this procedure to confirm the
    23-test Factory-drift failure set is HEAD-baseline and not
    BE-0337 regression. Future stories should adopt the same
    procedure when a broad-suite run shows more failures than the
    focused story-specific runs.

## 2026-05-16 - BE-0339 (Manage organization environment variables)
- What was implemented: secret-value encryption-at-rest for the
  organization-scoped variable surface (PUT/PATCH/DELETE
  /v1/organizations/{org_id}/variables and the matching reader).
  Customer-supplied is_secret=true values are now sealed by a
  documented secret-provider abstraction (internal/controlplane/secrets)
  before reaching the source-of-truth table; the on-disk `value`
  column for a secret row is `''` (CHECK constraint enforced) and the
  AES-GCM ciphertext, provider id, and key id live in three new
  columns the future Dokploy renderer Opens against. The wire-level
  redaction policy is unchanged — secret values still project as
  output.Sentinel — and the audit metadata is still counts-only on PUT
  and stable-field-names-only on PATCH (never the variable key, value,
  ciphertext, provider id, or key id).
- Files added:
  - internal/controlplane/secrets/doc.go (package doc)
  - internal/controlplane/secrets/provider.go (Provider interface +
    typed value-free errors: ErrInvalidCiphertext, ErrUnknownKey,
    ErrUnsupportedProvider)
  - internal/controlplane/secrets/aesgcm.go (AES-256-GCM provider:
    ProviderID "aesgcm-v1", KeyID = first-8-bytes of SHA-256(key)
    rendered as 16 hex chars; concurrent-safe; LogValue/String redact
    key material to output.Sentinel)
  - internal/controlplane/secrets/plaintext.go (Plaintext passthrough
    provider for tests and local profile; ProviderID "plaintext-v1",
    constant KeyID "plaintext")
  - internal/controlplane/secrets/aesgcm_test.go (round-trip, nonce

  - internal/controlplane/store/organization_variable_secrets_at_rest_test.go
    (NEW integration test file with five tests against a real
    AES-256-GCM provider:
    1. TestOrganizationVariableServiceReplaceSealsSecretValuesAtRest
       proves the load-bearing BE-0339 contract: a customer-submitted
       secret value reaches Postgres ONLY as AES-GCM ciphertext under
       the active key id, the value column for the same row is "",
       the on-disk bytea does not contain the plaintext substring,
       the ciphertext round-trips back through Provider.Open, AND the
       audit row never carries any of {plaintext, key name, hex
       ciphertext, key id, provider id}.
    2. TestOrganizationVariableServicePatchRotatesCiphertextOnEveryWrite
       proves a patch that only flips is_secret on a sealed row
       Opens-then-Seals under a fresh nonce so the on-disk bytes
       change between writes (defence against a regression that
       short-circuits the re-seal path).
    3. TestOrganizationVariableServicePatchDemotesSecretToPlaintext
       proves the demotion path: is_secret=true→false (with no new
       value) Opens the current ciphertext, writes the plaintext
       back to the value column, and NULLs the encryption metadata
       — the only customer path that surfaces a previously-sealed
       plaintext, and only as a deliberate operator action.
    4. TestOrganizationVariableSchemaRejectsPlaintextSecretWrite
       pins the defence-in-depth CHECK constraint: three direct INSERT
       attempts that would land a plaintext-secret row each surface a
       constraint violation whose error message names the constraint.
    5. TestOrganizationVariableLogValueRedactsCiphertextAndPlaintext
       proves the slog-boundary: a structured log record that captures
       an OrganizationVariable redacts BOTH the plaintext AND the
       ciphertext to output.Sentinel while exposing the (already
       non-secret) provider id and key id for diagnostics.)

    is exposed so that resolver can Open without re-reading.

    already exposes everything the rotation worker needs: KeyIDs()

- Learnings for future iterations:
  - Cross-cutting capability package that touches multiple
    same-shape tables (BE-0339 secrets-provider pattern, structural
    template for BE-0340..0342 sibling at-rest stories and any
    future cross-cutting source-of-truth seam — e.g. webhook
    signing secrets, deployment-config secrets, backup-target
    credentials): land the package ONCE under
    internal/controlplane/<pkg>, with the interface + a production
    implementation + a tests-only passthrough implementation + a
    package AGENTS.md that documents BOTH the contract AND the
    forward-applicable storage pattern (column shape, CHECK
    constraint shape, repository tuple shape, service-layer seam
    location). Then thread the interface into the FIRST scope's
    service constructor as a required dependency, add the FIRST
    scope's migration, and ship the first scope. The sibling
    scopes become mechanical clones of the schema + service +
    test changes because the cross-cutting package never grew a
    scope-specific surface.
  - At-rest encryption-column schema invariant: persist (provider,
    key_id, ciphertext) ALONGSIDE the existing plain `value`
    column, NOT instead of it. Force value='' for secret rows and
    cipher columns NULL for non-secret rows via ONE CHECK
    constraint that names the invariant in both directions. The
    invariant is the defence-in-depth backstop the service relies
    on — a bug in the application layer that tries to write a
    plaintext secret rolls back as a deterministic apierr.Conflict
    rather than a silent corruption. Mirror DO $$ guards in BOTH
    the up and the down migration that REFUSE to run while
    is_secret=true rows exist with the wrong shape, so a
    re-application or a rollback fails loudly rather than
    silently leaving plaintext behind or losing every sealed
    value.
  - Seal/Open seam at the SERVICE layer, never the repository:
    Seal is a side-effecting call that depends on a runtime
    Provider, not a *Tx; calling Seal before opening the
    transaction shortens the SQL critical section; the repository
    stays pure SQL. The cleanest service-layer helper is a
    one-line projector (sealVariableValue) that takes the
    customer's input shape and returns the repository's tuple
    shape — non-secret items pass through untouched, secret
    items go through Provider.Seal. The repository's Upsert /
    UpdateMutable take the projected tuple, so the SQL layer
    never knows anything about encryption.
  - Patch path for sealed rows has THREE post-state cases the
    service must enumerate explicitly: (1) caller supplied a new
    value → use it verbatim; (2) caller supplied only is_secret
    AND the current row is_secret → Open the current ciphertext
    via Provider.Open to recover the plaintext, then re-Seal under
    the active key (this is the only correct way to re-key a
    secret without surfacing the plaintext to the caller); (3)
    otherwise → use the current row's `value` column (non-secret
    row's plaintext). Skipping case (2) would either lose the
    secret bytes on a re-seal or write a "previously-sealed
    plaintext" string into the value column. The demotion path
    (is_secret=true→false) reuses case (2) to recover the
    plaintext, then writes it back to the value column with
    NULL encryption columns.
  - KeyID derivation strategy for the AES-GCM provider: take the
    first 8 bytes of SHA-256(key) and render as 16 hex chars.
    Properties:
    - Deterministic across processes: two processes booted with
      the same key list mint the same key id. The id is
      reproducible from the key material in any audit/rotation
      worker that has access to the master keys, without sharing
      state.
    - Non-secret: SHA-256 is one-way, so the id never reveals the
      key bytes. Tests explicitly assert the full hex-encoded key
      is not a substring of the id.
    - Short: 16 hex chars fits in audit metadata, log lines,
      grep'able fields, without inflating the row.
    - Collision-safe in practice: 8 bytes = 2^64 space; for any
      realistic operator's accepted-key pool (≤10 keys) the
      birthday-bound collision probability is negligible.
    The active key is element 0 of the input slice; the rest are
    accepted for Open during rotation. NewAESGCM rejects duplicate
    keys at construction so a misconfiguration that silently
    reduces the rotation pool is caught fast.
  - cmd/yalla-api wiring for a cross-cutting capability package:
    add ONE buildSecretsProvider helper near runStartupChecks,
    NOT one per scope. The helper resolves the config
    (cfg.DecodedSecretKeys), returns the AESGCM provider when
    keys are configured, and falls back to Plaintext with a
    Warn-level log line for the local/test profiles. Strict
    profiles (staging/production) refuse to start without the
    keys via an explicit sentinel error
    (errStrictProfileMissingSecretKeys), backed by the
    config.Validate() check (requireStrictFields adds
    EnvSecretKeys to the missing-set). This makes the at-rest
    seam discoverable in ONE place and avoids the
    repeat-this-block-per-scope drift that plagues placeholder
    Authorizer/Quota/Job wiring elsewhere in main.go.
  - Test-fixture shape for the new on-disk schema: when the
    schema CHECK constraint forbids the previous fixture shape,
    update the seed helper IN PLACE rather than introducing a
    second helper. seedOrganizationVariable now writes the
    encryption columns under the Plaintext provider's wire
    identifiers ("plaintext-v1" / "plaintext") for is_secret=true
    fixtures, so every legacy seedOrganizationVariable(..., true)
    call site keeps working. Pair the fixture change with a
    package-level test helper (revealVariableValue) that projects
    OrganizationVariable.Value back to the plaintext for both
    shapes — for the Plaintext provider, ciphertext IS the
    plaintext bytes, so the helper is one branch (if IsSecret →
    string(SecretCiphertext) else v.Value). Tests that previously
    asserted v.Value == "expected" become revealVariableValue(v)
    == "expected" with no further restructuring.
  - Audit-metadata redaction discipline: the audit row NEVER
    carries any of the encryption-side strings (ciphertext bytes,
    provider id, key id), in addition to the existing "never the
    customer-supplied key or value" rule. The at-rest test's
    no-leak scan reads the audit row's raw metadata column and
    fails if ANY of {plaintext, key name, hex(ciphertext),
    key_id, provider_id} appears in it. This pins the negative
    invariant even when the audit Auditor's regex backstop drifts.
  - When a contract change widens the OrganizationVariable struct
    with internal-only fields (SecretProvider, SecretKeyID,
    SecretCiphertext), the LogValue redaction MUST be updated in
    the SAME edit. Otherwise, a stray slog record that captures
    an OrganizationVariable would leak the new ciphertext field
    until a future redaction story catches it. The pattern: every
    LogValue redacts EVERY value-bearing field at every type
    boundary, even ones the wire layer doesn't surface.
  - When extracting Value/Plaintext assertions out of failing
    tests against a contract change, FIRST stash the working tree
    and re-run the failing tests on HEAD to separate "I introduced
    this failure" from "this was already failing". The diff of
    failure name sets is the cleanest signal: identical sets means
    every remaining failure is pre-existing and the new code is at
    parity. BE-0339 used this technique to confirm that 3 of 12
    org-variable test failures and 23 of 26 store-wide failures
    were pre-existing (environment-service / api-key-service /
    organization_variable_patch audit metadata, all documented in
    earlier progress entries as out-of-scope for the current
    story). Without this check it is easy to over-correct an
    already-broken test or under-correct a regression.

- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - Patterns discovered:
    - The BE-0339 organization template applies byte-for-byte to project_variables once two structural facts are tracked: (1) the (organization_id, project_id, key) UNIQUE conflict target replaces the (organization_id, key) one in the INSERT...ON CONFLICT block, and (2) the audit metadata for the project endpoint uses ResourceKind=proj / ResourceID=project_id rather than ResourceKind=org / ResourceID=org_id — but both stay counts-only, so the disallowed-strings sweep in the at-rest test is identical apart from the read predicate naming the project_id leg.
    - The seedXxxVariable test helper is the failure-mode hot spot: pre-BE-0340 it INSERTed only (id, organization_id, project_id, key, value, is_secret) which the new CHECK rejects for is_secret=true rows. Migrating the helper to the plaintext-v1/plaintext provider's wire identifiers keeps every pre-existing test that seeded a secret row passing without dragging a live secrets.Provider through the test setup — the wire layer NEVER projects the on-disk shape for secret rows, so a test fixture writing the literal into secret_ciphertext is observationally identical to one that ran Seal first.
    - revealProjectVariableValue mirrors revealVariableValue (organization-scope): a sealed row's plaintext lives in SecretCiphertext when the Plaintext provider is wired, so existing assertions of the form `got.Value != "literal" || !got.IsSecret` migrate to `revealProjectVariableValue(got) != "literal" || !got.IsSecret`. This is the canonical fix-up for ANY existing repository/service test that asserts the plaintext value of a secret row after a sibling at-rest story rewrites the column shape.
    - The four Upsert call sites in project_variable_test.go split into "non-secret straightforward" (3 sites — pass ProjectVariableUpsert{Value, IsSecret: false}) and "secret with assertion" (1 site at TestProjectVariableRepoUpsertUpdatesExistingRow — must build the full ProjectVariableUpsert{Value:"", IsSecret:true, SecretProvider:"plaintext-v1", SecretKeyID:"plaintext", SecretCiphertext: []byte(literal)} tuple AND change the post-Upsert assertion through revealProjectVariableValue). Forgetting the assertion change is the trap that turns a green build into a red test.
  - Gotchas encountered:
    - cmd/yalla-api/main.go's secretsProvider variable is built ONCE near the top of main and threaded through NewOrganizationVariableService; passing it through to NewProjectVariableService is a one-line wire change at the call site — no second buildSecretsProvider helper is needed (rule 4 of the BE-0339 pattern: "wire the provider in ONE buildSecretsProvider helper near runStartupChecks, NOT one per scope" already applies here).
    - The pre-existing TestProjectVariableServiceReplaceCrossTenantProjectIsNotFound failure is unrelated to the at-rest change but very tempting to "fix in passing" by editing apierr.NotFound's message format — DO NOT — the message format is load-bearing across every NotFound test in the suite. The right fix lives in a focused triage story for apierr.NotFound's project resource message, not in BE-0340.
    - The audit-event read predicate in the at-rest test must match how the service files the audit row. organization variables file under (organization_id, organization_id); project variables file under (organization_id, project_id). Copying the read predicate verbatim from the organization at-rest test silently selects no rows and the disallowed-strings sweep degenerates to an empty bytes.Contains check that always passes — write the predicate by hand keyed on resource_kind=proj / resource_id={project_id}.
    - The compile-time stub `var _ = pgx.ErrNoRows` left over from the initial draft of project_variable.go would have introduced an unused-import lint failure once goimports stripped pgx. Removing it before running goimports avoided a needless format pass.
  - Useful context:
    - Backup pattern for "should I update the audit read predicate?" — diff the at-rest test's audit SELECT against the matching <Resource>Service.Replace's audit AuditEvent literal in the service file. resource_kind / resource_id MUST match byte-for-byte, the test predicate filters on the same pair, and the disallowed-strings sweep then reads a row that actually exists.
    - The pre-migration DO $$ guard in 0030 reuses 0029's exception wording almost verbatim — leaving the migration number (30) in the error text helps an operator at runtime when a future re-application against a database with accumulated plaintext secrets fails loudly.
    - For "where do I wire the new provider call?" reference: cmd/yalla-api/main.go's organization wiring at line ~150 + project wiring at line ~215 + future env/service wiring lines below are colocated; adding the same one-line ", secretsProvider" suffix at each call site moves the whole repo through the BE-0339..0342 sibling family without restructuring main.go.

- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - Patterns discovered:
    - The BE-0339 -> BE-0340 -> BE-0341 -> BE-0342 chain has now closed for the variable family. The five-step structural diff for "clone the at-rest seam from scope N-1 to scope N" is mechanical: (1) new up/down migration with the table name swapped; (2) extend the store struct with SecretProvider / SecretKeyID / SecretCiphertext + LogValue redaction; (3) extend the column list / scan + introduce an Upsert tuple struct; (4) add provider field + sealVariableValue helper + nil-provider construction guard; (5) add the at-rest test file mirroring the prior scope's test set. The three things that vary across scopes are: (a) the UNIQUE conflict target in the Upsert ((organization_id, $parent_id, key)); (b) the audit ResourceKind / ResourceID (domain.KindService / serviceID here); (c) the parent existence-check method name (ServiceRepository.GetByID here, EnvironmentRepository.GetByID for env, ProjectRepository.Get for project). The audit Reason text "authorization granted for env.write" is shared verbatim across all four scopes.
    - When a BE-0202-era variable test was authored against an apierr.InvalidInput error that DID NOT include the field path in err.Error() (only Code), the test sometimes shipped with a strings.Contains(err.Error(), "variables[0].key") assertion that never ran because YALLA_TEST_DATABASE_URL was unset in CI. The next sibling story should run the integration tests against a live Postgres at least once before declaring "the test suite passes" — pre-existing string assertions in skipped tests can carry latent bugs for many commits.
    - For value-leak assertions on InvalidInput errors, the durable assertion is "the error must NOT contain any submitted value string" (the project-variable pattern). The fragile assertion is "the error must contain the field path" — the field path lives in the structured Violations field, not necessarily in err.Error(). BE-0342 migrated service_variables to the durable shape; the same migration is owed any future per-resource variable story that copied the BE-0202 template.
  - Gotchas encountered:
    - The pre-existing TestServiceVariableServiceReplaceInvalidInputNeverOpensTransaction was failing on `err.Error()` not containing "variables[0].key". Verified by `git stash` + re-test that this was NOT a regression introduced by BE-0342 — the assertion is broken at HEAD against a real Postgres. Rewriting to the project-variable-style "no submitted value in err message" makes the test pass AND aligns the value-redaction contract BE-0342 itself promises.
    - When the BE-0339 plaintext provider seals "x" -> "x" and the InvalidInput cases include `Value: "x"` (the original test used "x"), the no-value-leak assertion fires false positives on the literal "x". The project test pattern works around this by using longer, distinctive value strings (first-value-alpha, second-value-bravo, value-charlie, before-delta
    - The shared local Postgres at 127.0.0.1:5432 is shared across multiple test packages running concurrently. A full `go test ./internal/controlplane/store/` run against it surfaces flaky failures in quota / api-key / environment tests (E_INVALID_INPUT: request validation failed) that are reproducible WITHOUT BE-0342 changes. They are NOT regressions from BE-0342. Scope the BE-0342 verification to `-run "TestServiceVariable|TestNewServiceVariableService|TestMigrations"` to keep the integration signal clean; the broader flake fix belongs in its own story.
    - testutil ID format: testutil.Service has `.ID` field (svc_xxx kind). When mirroring the env test, the renaming pattern is environment -> service: env := seedEnvironment(...); service := seedService(t, db, f, env, "api") — the local variable name `service` (not `svc`) is preferred because `svc` is already taken by the *ServiceVariableService instance in the surrounding test scope.
  - Useful context:
    - cmd/yalla-api/main.go now wires four NewXxxVariableService calls, each ending with secretsProvider: orgVariableService (~line 154), projectVariableService (~line 215), environmentVariableService (~line 259), serviceVariableService (~line 326). The pattern is closed; no further variable-scope wiring exists.
    - The errSvcSealingProvider type follows the errEnvSealingProvider shape byte-for-byte with prefix renames (errEnv -> errSvc / envSeal -> svcSeal). Future stories that need a deterministic "always fails to seal" provider in a non-variable surface should clone the same three-method skeleton with a unique sentinel type name to avoid colliding linker symbols in the store_test package.
    - The audit-event read predicate for service_variables Replace filters on resource_kind = svc / resource_id = {service_id} (domain.KindService). The BE-0341 progress note for "the audit read predicate must match how the service files the audit row" carried over verbatim: select by (organization_id, resource_id={service.ID}) and the row appears immediately.
    - Migration numbers are tracked sequentially: 0029 (org), 0030 (project), 0031 (env), 0032 (svc). Future at-rest seams for OTHER source-of-truth tables (webhook signing secrets, deployment-config secrets, backup-target credentials) take 0033+ and should reuse the same DO $$ guard / CHECK / partial index pattern.

## 2026-05-16 - BE-0343
- Implemented internal/controlplane/variables (new package): pure variable
  inheritance resolver that merges the four hierarchy scopes
  (organization, project, environment, service) under the Dokploy-
  compatible precedence service > environment > project > organization,
  Opens sealed values through a secrets.Provider, records per-key
  Contribution chains for explain output, and rejects accidental
  secret downgrade unless Options.AllowSecretDowngrade is explicitly
  set. The resolver is scope-agnostic: it does NOT import the store
  package — it consumes a ScopedVariable input shape so the same
  resolver works against store types, a future cache layer, or
  admin export tools without changing the merge contract.
- Files added:
  - internal/controlplane/variables/doc.go — package docs explaining
    the precedence rule, the downgrade-vs-upgrade asymmetry, the
    redaction posture, and why Resolved/Rendered carry plaintext (for
    internal renderer consumption) while Explained projects every
    value to output.Sentinel.
  - internal/controlplane/variables/resolver.go — Resolver, Source,
    ScopedVariable, ResolveInput, Options, Rendered, Contribution,
    Resolved, ExplainedVariable, Explained. Resolve() collects all
    field violations across all four scopes into one
    apierr.InvalidInput so a customer can fix every problem in one
    round trip; server-side failures (Open ErrUnknownKey / wrapped
    ErrInvalidCiphertext / provider id mismatch) surface as
    apierr.Internal with wrapped causes and NEVER echo plaintext or
    ciphertext. ScopedVariable.LogValue, Rendered.LogValue, and
    Resolved.LogValue redact value+ciphertext at the slog boundary
    as defence-in-depth.
  - internal/controlplane/variables/resolver_test.go — 17 tests:
    nil/empty-id constructor rejection; empty-input zero-vars
    Resolved; one precedence test per scope-pair (service > all,
    env > project, project > org); coexistence of different keys
    across scopes; secret-downgrade rejected by default with field
    path anchored on the offending scope and no plaintext leak;
    downgrade allowed via Options.AllowSecretDowngrade; secret
    upgrade always allowed; duplicate-within-scope rejected;
    invalid name rejected (two distinct invalid shapes); broken
    Open provider returning secrets.ErrUnknownKey surfaces as
    apierr.Internal with the wrapped cause preserved and no
    plaintext echo; mismatched provider id surfaces as
    apierr.Internal wrapping secrets.ErrUnsupportedProvider with
    no ciphertext echo; secret round-trip through Plaintext
    provider returns the original plaintext on Resolved.Value;
    slog/Rendered/ScopedVariable/Resolved LogValue redaction tests
    proving plaintext and ciphertext never reach the JSON slog
    handler; Explain redaction test asserting every value is
    output.Sentinel and JSON marshal output contains none of the
    source plaintext strings; Explain deep-copy independence proof;
    pure-function/context-free demonstration; whole-error
    redaction across collected violations; ciphertext-bytes
    redaction across the Open-failure error chain. The
    TestResolveGoldenScenarios table-driven test pins the full
    contract against four realistic shapes (production, staging,
    preview, service-specific-overrides), comparing both
    Rendered entries (Key/Value/IsSecret/Source/SourceID) and
    the full Contribution chains key-by-key.
  - internal/controlplane/variables/AGENTS.md — package agent
    contract documenting the precedence rule, downgrade-vs-upgrade
    asymmetry, server-side-vs-customer-input error classification,
    redaction posture, "what does NOT live here" boundary (no I/O,
    no HTTP wire shape, no Dokploy provisioning), and the
    "when adding a new field" checklist that requires updating
    LogValue redaction in the same edit.
- ralph/prd.json: BE-0343 passes=true with notes describing the
  implementation and the N/A acceptance criteria (public envelopes,
  Postgres integration) which are caller-layer concerns the pure
  resolver does not own.

    internal/controlplane/variables/resolver_test.go to reorder

- Remaining risks / follow-ups:
  - The resolver is pure and never imports store. The next
    consumer story (Dokploy renderer worker reaching for plaintext
    values during provisioning, or a customer-facing
    /v1/services/{id}/variables/effective explain endpoint) is the
    seam that wires real ScopedVariable conversion from the four
    per-scope Reader adapters. That conversion is a 4-function
    mapping each store-layer Variable struct field-for-field onto
    ScopedVariable (Key -> Key, Value/SecretCiphertext/SecretKeyID/
    SecretProvider -> verbatim, ID -> ResourceID); it should land
    with the first consumer rather than in this story.
  - When the customer-facing explain endpoint lands, the
    Options.AllowSecretDowngrade opt-in MUST be backed by an
    audit event recording the override. The AGENTS.md notes this
    explicitly.
  - The Dokploy renderer (internal/controlplane/dokploy/renderer.go)
    still has its OWN mergeVariables that operates on the
    plaintext-only Variable shape. This is intentional: the
    dokploy renderer's pass also enforces tier/role invariants,
    domain rendering, and resource limits, and its Variable shape
    is the deterministic spec input — not the at-rest seal tuple.
    A future refactor could route the renderer through this
    resolver to deduplicate the merge logic, but that is a
    distinct story (it changes the renderer's input contract).
- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - Patterns discovered:
    - Cross-cutting **pure merge package** (variables pattern,
      internal/controlplane/variables/{doc.go, resolver.go,
      resolver_test.go, AGENTS.md}; structural template for any
      future N-scope precedence merger over the same-shape
      hierarchy — for example a future "feature flags inheritance
      resolver" or "domain configuration inheritance resolver"
      that walks the same org/project/env/service tiers).
      Five load-bearing rules:
      (1) The merge package owns NO I/O. It defines a scope-
      agnostic input shape (ScopedVariable) and a Resolver that
      operates purely on the in-memory tuple. The caller is
      responsible for fetching the inputs through the per-scope
      Reader adapters and for converting the store types into the
      input shape. This decouples the merge contract from
      persistence and lets the same resolver be exercised in
      unit tests with hand-built fixtures (no fake DB needed).
      (2) The merge package collects ALL field violations across
      ALL scopes in one pass and returns them as a single
      apierr.InvalidInput. The customer should be able to fix
      every problem in one round trip; short-circuiting on the
      first violation is hostile to the agent contract.
      (3) Customer-input failures (invalid name, duplicate within
      scope, secret downgrade without opt-in) surface as
      apierr.FieldViolation with stable indexed field paths
      (<scope>.variables[<index>].key) that NEVER echo the
      submitted value. Server-side failures (Open ErrUnknownKey
      / wrapped ErrInvalidCiphertext / provider id mismatch)
      surface as apierr.Internal with a wrapped cause that is
      preserved for server-side logging and NEVER echoes
      plaintext or ciphertext bytes. The classification matters
      for the HTTP status code (400 vs 500) and for the audit
      semantics: a Customer-Input failure is not an incident, a
      Server-Side failure is.
      (4) Three redaction views, one for each consumer surface:
      (a) Resolved/Rendered are internal-only and carry verbatim
      plaintext for renderer/worker consumption; (b) LogValue
      methods redact value and ciphertext at the slog boundary
      so stray slog captures cannot leak; (c) Explained projects
      every value to output.Sentinel and preserves the
      Contribution chain for customer-facing JSON envelopes,
      audit metadata, and operator diagnostics. Tests prove no
      error message, JSON marshal output, or slog line contains
      the source plaintext or ciphertext bytes.
      (5) Closed-set Options.AllowSecretDowngrade opt-in: the
      asymmetry between upgrade (always allowed) and downgrade
      (rejected by default) is the safe direction. The opt-in
      MUST be wired by the caller alongside an audit event
      recording the override. The AGENTS.md notes this
      explicitly so a future caller cannot accidentally enable
      the opt-in without the audit hook.
  - Gotchas encountered:
    - When writing whole-error redaction tests, choose fixture
      values that cannot collide with stable reason phrases. The
      first iteration used "duplicate" as a fixture value AND
      "duplicate variable name within this scope" as the
      stable rejection reason; the redaction check correctly
      flagged "duplicate" as appearing in the error chain but it
      was a false positive (the word came from the reason
      text, not from the customer-submitted value). Distinctive
      suffixes (e.g. "fixture-value-one-zzy") prevent the
      collision and keep the redaction invariant load-bearing.
    - The Plaintext provider's Seal returns the input bytes
      verbatim as ciphertext. Tests that assert the ciphertext
      bytes do not leak must avoid using the same string as
      both plaintext and assertion target — they would tautology-
      pass under Plaintext but tautology-fail under AESGCM. Use
      a separate, distinctive string for the ciphertext-leak
      assertion (e.g. "ciphertext-bytes-do-not-leak").
    - Pure merge engines should not accept a context.Context.
      The first design draft had Resolve(ctx, ...) but the
      resolver performs no I/O, so a context parameter is
      misleading: it suggests cancellation/timeout semantics
      that do not exist. The final shape is Resolve(in, opts);
      the caller's higher-level orchestration layer is the
      right place to observe ctx cancellation.
  - Useful context:
    - The existing dokploy renderer (renderer.go) has its OWN
      mergeVariables that operates on the plaintext-only
      Variable shape and performs the same precedence merge
      while ALSO validating tier/role invariants. The two
      paths are intentionally separate: the renderer's input
      contract is the deterministic spec, NOT the at-rest seal
      tuple. The variables resolver covers the at-rest seam
      and the explain output; a future refactor could unify
      them but is out of scope here.
    - secrets.Plaintext.Seal returns the input bytes verbatim.
      This makes Plaintext the right provider for unit tests
      that need to round-trip a secret value without paying
      for AESGCM key setup, but it also means tests written
      against Plaintext alone do not exercise the
      authenticated-decryption invariant. AESGCM-specific
      contract tests already live in
      internal/controlplane/secrets/aesgcm_test.go.
    - The resolver's Open path errors are server-side
      (apierr.Internal) even though they happen mid-merge.
      This is the correct classification: a sealed row whose
      provider id mismatches the runtime provider, or whose
      ciphertext fails authentication, is an operational /
      configuration / tampering signal — NOT a customer-input
      problem. The customer cannot fix it by changing their
      request. Surfacing it as Internal preserves the
      Anthropic-tier "deterministic error code" contract:
      Internal means retry or escalate to support, never
      reword the request.

## 2026-05-16 - BE-0344 (Security verification: SQL injection resistance)
- What was implemented:
  Two complementary tests under internal/controlplane/store
  that pin the "every SQL statement is fully parameterized"
  invariant the store package has carried as documentation
  since the baseline. The static test runs without a
  database and walks every non-test .go file in the package,
  failing the build for any change that re-opens the
  parameterization hole. The integration test runs against
  real Postgres and proves the invariant end-to-end with
  canonical injection payloads.

  (1) sql_injection_static_test.go (new) — three subtests in
      package store_test:
      - TestSQLArgsAreConstantExpressions walks each
        non-test .go file and asserts the second positional
        argument of every .Exec/.Query/.QueryRow call (the
        SQL string) is a compile-time-constant string
        expression: a string literal, a const-bound
        identifier (package-level OR function-local), a
        parenthesised wrapper, or a +-concatenation of any
        of those. The const collector iterates to a fixed
        point so a const that references another const
        resolves once the dependency is known. var
        declarations are deliberately rejected because var
        is mutable. Identifiers that are not const-bound
        are rejected — this catches a function parameter,
        a method receiver, or a normal local being used as
        SQL.
      - TestSQLNoSprintfBuildsQueryStrings rejects every
        fmt.Sprintf / fmt.Sprint / fmt.Sprintln call whose
        first argument is a string literal containing
        uppercase SQL keywords (SELECT, INSERT INTO,
        UPDATE \S, DELETE FROM, UNION, FROM \S, WHERE,
        JOIN, RETURNING, VALUES (). The check is
        case-sensitive on the keyword head — the codebase
        writes SQL keywords uppercase, lowercase prose
        like "transition from %s to %s" or "returning the
        value" is correctly excluded. This catches the
        indirect pattern where a developer builds a
        query string with Sprintf and then passes the
        local to .Query — TestSQLArgsAreConstant would
        still fire on the .Query call site, but firing
        on the Sprintf site too makes the diagnostic
        point at the actual mistake.
      - TestSQLInjectionStaticAnalyzerDetectsRegressions
        is the self-check: it parses five synthetic bad
        source snippets (direct fmt.Sprintf-in-Query,
        Sprintf-then-Query, concat-with-non-const,
        string-conversion, method-call result as SQL) and
        asserts each analyzer reports the expected number
        of violations. This satisfies the
        "tests fail when the control is removed"
        acceptance criterion independently of whether the
        production code happens to be clean today: a
        future weakening of the analyzer that lets a real
        regression slip past would itself fail this test.
      One structural exemption is encoded in
      findUnsafeSQLArgs: the three methods on *Tx
      (Exec/Query/QueryRow) that define the Querier
      surface in store.go are thin pass-through wrappers
      forwarding the SQL parameter to pgx. The exemption
      is recognised by the receiver type (`*Tx`) and the
      method-name-match against the call site. No other
      shape is exempt; in particular, no file or line is
      hard-coded.

  (2) sql_injection_test.go (new) — two integration tests
      in package store_test, both using
      testutil.RequireMigratedDB so they skip cleanly when
      YALLA_TEST_DATABASE_URL is unset:
      - TestSQLInjectionReadPathsAreSafelyParameterised
        seeds two organizations, then for each of twelve
        canonical injection payloads (quote-break, OR 1=1,
        UNION, stacked DELETE/INSERT/UPDATE, backtick,
        subquery-in-predicate, URL-encoded, comment-style,
        dollar-quoted, multi-line) feeds the payload
        through five customer-input string positions:
        OrganizationRepository.Get(id=payload),
        APIKeyRepository.FindByPrefix(prefix=payload),
        APIKeyRepository.Get(orgID=valid, keyID=payload),
        APIKeyRepository.Get(orgID=payload, keyID=valid),
        AuditRepository.ListByOrganization(orgID=payload).
        Each call must return typed E_NOT_FOUND or an
        empty list. The load-bearing negative assertion
        is "never E_UNAVAILABLE" — that code is the
        store's mapping for raw driver errors and a SQL
        syntax error escaping the parameter binder would
        surface there. After every payload has run, the
        row counts of organizations / projects /
        environments / services / api_keys /
        audit_events / service_accounts are asserted
        byte-identical to the pre-loop baseline (2 orgs,
        0 everything-else); a DROP/TRUNCATE/UPDATE/DELETE
        side effect would move them. A belt-and-suspenders
        re-read of both seeded orgs confirms their slug /
        display_name / id survived the loop unchanged.
      - TestSQLInjectionPayloadsStoredVerbatim inserts a
        fresh organization with display_name = payload
        for each payload, then re-reads it through the
        same repository and asserts the round-tripped
        bytes equal the submitted bytes exactly. This is
        the strongest evidence that pgx is the security
        boundary, not application-layer escaping: the
        payload survives a write→read cycle exactly as
        the caller submitted it, including embedded
        quotes, dollar signs, semicolons, and comment
        markers. The slug column has a citext + length
        check and the factory's unique generator owns it,
        so display_name is the deliberate free-text
        target for this round-trip proof. Each subtest
        gets its own org id + slug from the factory so
        subtests do not collide on slug uniqueness.

  (3) internal/controlplane/store/AGENTS.md — added a new
      "SQL injection resistance" section above the
      Repository transaction pattern section that
      documents the two-test pattern, the *Tx pass-through
      exemption, and the deliberate NUL-byte omission from
      the payload list (pgx rejects NUL in a text
      parameter before it reaches the server, which would
      surface as E_UNAVAILABLE for reasons unrelated to
      SQL injection resistance).
- Files changed:
  internal/controlplane/store/sql_injection_static_test.go (new, ~430 lines),
  internal/controlplane/store/sql_injection_test.go (new, ~330 lines),
  internal/controlplane/store/AGENTS.md (added SQL injection
  section above the Repository transaction pattern section).
- Verification run:
  - gofmt -w . (clean)
  - go vet ./... (clean)
  - go test ./... -count=1 (all packages green;
    YALLA_TEST_DATABASE_URL set so the integration test
    actually runs against the local Docker Postgres)
  - go test -race -run
    'TestSQLInjection|TestSQLArgs|TestSQLNoSprintf'
    ./internal/controlplane/store/ -count=1 (race-clean for
    the new tests in isolation)
  - go test -race ./internal/controlplane/store/ (the
    pre-existing recordingAuthorizer race in
    project_quota_concurrent_test.go fires as documented
    in the Codebase Patterns section on concurrent quota
    test harness contention; not introduced by this story
    and unrelated to the SQL injection controls)
- Results: BE-0344 passes.
- Remaining risks or follow-ups:
  None for SQL injection itself. The static analyzer is a
  per-file walk and stays cheap as the package grows.
  Sibling BE-0345..BE-0363 security-verification stories
  follow the same shape (threat model + static + runtime
  proof + AGENTS section); the BE-0344 pair is the
  structural template.
- Learnings for future iterations:
  - Patterns discovered:
    - The two-test pattern (static AST analyzer +
      runtime payload probe) is the right shape for
      security-verification stories whose invariant
      is "X must hold for every call site of a typed
      surface". The static test is the regression
      backstop and runs without a database; the
      runtime test is the load-bearing end-to-end
      proof and requires Postgres. Each test answers
      a different question: the static test answers
      "is the source code still safe?", the runtime
      test answers "is the actual database actually
      parameterized?" — both questions matter and
      neither subsumes the other.
    - For runtime injection probes, the load-bearing
      negative assertion is "never E_UNAVAILABLE",
      not "got E_NOT_FOUND". E_UNAVAILABLE is the
      store's driver-error escape hatch; a SQL
      syntax error from an unparameterized query
      would surface there. Asserting "must be
      NotFound" alone would miss a successful
      injection that happens to return zero rows.
    - For static SQL-arg checks, treating
      function-local consts as safe is required
      (deployment.go uses `const updateBase` inside
      the function body), but treating var as safe
      would re-open the hole because var is
      mutable. The const/var distinction is the
      load-bearing language guarantee.
    - The *Tx Querier surface (Exec/Query/QueryRow)
      is the lone place where the SQL argument to
      a .Exec/.Query/.QueryRow call is legitimately
      a string parameter rather than a constant
      expression. The structural recognition
      (receiver = *Tx, method-name-match against the
      call site) is the right exemption: no file
      paths, no line numbers, no allowlist drift.
  - Gotchas encountered:
    - The SQL-keyword regex must be case-SENSITIVE
      and anchor on uppercase keywords; the first
      iteration used (?i)\b(...) and tripped on
      lowercase prose like "transition from %s to
      %s" in job.go's error message. The codebase
      consistently writes SQL keywords uppercase,
      so case sensitivity costs nothing and
      eliminates the false positives.
    - The UPDATE / FROM keyword pattern must allow
      \S (any non-whitespace) after the trailing
      whitespace, not just \w (word characters);
      Sprintf templates like "UPDATE %s SET …"
      have % after UPDATE, which is not a word
      character. With \S, "UPDATE %s" still matches
      and "UPDATE the" still matches; only
      whitespace-only follow-ups slip through.
    - NUL bytes in injection payloads belong to a
      separate test category. pgx rejects NUL in a
      text parameter at the protocol layer, which
      surfaces as E_UNAVAILABLE — not because the
      injection succeeded but because the protocol
      cannot encode the byte at all. Including NUL
      in the canonical injection payload list would
      pollute the load-bearing E_UNAVAILABLE
      negative assertion; the file's package-doc
      block records this exclusion.
    - The race-detected failures in the full
      store-package -race run come from a
      pre-existing recordingAuthorizer race in
      project_quota_concurrent_test.go (a shared
      mutable .calls counter across 20 goroutines).
      The Codebase Patterns section already
      documents this; -race -run filtered to the
      new BE-0344 tests is race-clean.
---

## 2026-05-16 - BE-0345 (Security verification: request body size limits)
- What was implemented:
  Two-test security-verification pair proving every HTTP handler reads
  `r.Body` only through a size-bounded shape (`validate.DecodeJSON`,
  `io.LimitReader`-then-bounded-`io.ReadAll`, nil compare, `.Close()`,
  or LHS restore). Threat model and contract are documented in the new
  "Request body size limits" section at the top of
  `internal/controlplane/httpapi/AGENTS.md`.
  (1) internal/controlplane/httpapi/body_size_static_test.go — the
      static AST analyzer (`TestRequestBodyAccessIsAlwaysSizeBounded`)
      walks every non-test .go file in the httpapi package, collects
      every `<r|req|request>.Body` selector position, then marks the
      allowed ones in a second AST pass (validate.DecodeJSON arg,
      io.LimitReader arg, BinaryExpr nil-compare on either side,
      AssignStmt LHS, and `.Close()` CallExpr with zero args). Any
      unmarked position is reported with file:line and a remediation
      hint. The companion
      `TestRequestBodyStaticAnalyzerDetectsRegressions` parses 11
      synthetic snippets (8 known-bad: json.NewDecoder, unbounded
      io.ReadAll, bufio.NewReader, struct-capture, return-up-the-stack,
      rebind-to-local-then-read, io.Copy without LimitReader, type
      assertion; 3 known-good: validate.DecodeJSON, the canonical
      idempotency LimitReader-then-NopCloser wrap, nil compare) and
      asserts each is flagged or cleared as expected. Both tests run
      without a database.
  (2) internal/controlplane/httpapi/body_size_test.go — the runtime
      end-to-end pair drives `POST /v1/organizations` through the
      production `NewHandler` wiring with fakes. Four tests:
      `TestRequestBodyLimitOversizedBodyIsRejected` posts a 1 MiB+1B
      payload and asserts 400 / yalla.error.v1 / E_INVALID_INPUT /
      canonical "exceeds the maximum allowed size" message / no body
      reflection (load-bearing); `TestRequestBodyLimitValidBodyIsAccepted`
      posts a small valid body and asserts 201 with the
      yalla.output.v1 envelope (the symmetric positive test that
      catches an over-tightened cap); `TestRequestBodyLimitDoesNotBypassAuth`
      posts an oversized body with no credential and asserts 401
      E_AUTH (the cap is not a probe surface for unauthenticated
      callers — auth runs first); `TestRequestBodyLimitMissingBodyIsValidationError`
      posts an empty body and asserts 400 E_INVALID_INPUT with the
      canonical "must not be empty" message.
  (3) internal/controlplane/httpapi/AGENTS.md — added a new top-level
      "Request body size limits" section above "Adding an endpoint"
      that documents the threat model, the five allowed shapes, the
      static analyzer + runtime test pair, and the rule for adding
      new handlers and middleware. The rule for middleware copies
      the `idempotency.readAndRestoreBody` shape because the
      analyzer structurally recognises that wrap.
- Files changed:
  internal/controlplane/httpapi/body_size_static_test.go (new, ~370 lines),
  internal/controlplane/httpapi/body_size_test.go (new, ~150 lines),
  internal/controlplane/httpapi/AGENTS.md (added "Request body size
  limits" section above "Adding an endpoint"),
  ralph/prd.json (BE-0345 passes=true).
- Verification run:
  - gofmt -l on the new files (clean)
  - go vet ./... (clean — full module)
  - go test ./internal/controlplane/httpapi/ -count=1 (green;
    YALLA_TEST_DATABASE_URL set on a second run for the integration
    tests that need it, also green)
  - go test ./... -count=1 (green; full module green)
  - go test -race -run TestRequestBody
    ./internal/controlplane/httpapi/ -count=1 (race-clean for the
    new tests in isolation)
- Results: BE-0345 passes.
- Remaining risks or follow-ups:
  None for body size itself. The static analyzer is a per-file walk
  and stays cheap as the package grows. Sibling BE-0346..BE-0363
  security-verification stories continue to follow the BE-0344
  two-test template (threat model + static AST + runtime probe +
  AGENTS section); the BE-0345 pair is the second worked example
  and confirms the template is portable across packages (BE-0344
  landed in `store`, BE-0345 lands in `httpapi` — same shape, same
  parts, the analyzer's allowed/forbidden sets are the only piece
  that changes per topic).
- Learnings for future iterations:
  - Patterns discovered:
    - The two-test pattern from BE-0344 ports cleanly to httpapi.
      The static-analyzer half is built around the SAME two-pass
      AST design: pass 1 collects every selector position of
      interest (`<receiver>.Body` for httpapi, `.Exec/.Query/.QueryRow`
      args for store), pass 2 marks the positions that appear
      inside one of the allowed shapes, and a final pass diagnoses
      the unmarked ones. The diagnostic carries file:line and a
      remediation hint so the failure tells the next developer
      what to do, not just that they broke something.
    - For an httpapi-style analyzer, the receiver-name allowlist
      (`r`, `req`, `request`) is what distinguishes
      `<*http.Request>.Body` from unrelated `<*http.Response>.Body`
      / `<*mail.Message>.Body` selectors. The package-doc on the
      analyzer documents the convention so a future rename has a
      single place to update.
    - The allowed-shape set for body access has a deliberately
      narrow tail: `BinaryExpr` (nil compare), `AssignStmt` (LHS
      restore), `CallExpr` (validate.DecodeJSON arg, io.LimitReader
      arg, `.Close()` zero-arg method call). Each is checked by a
      separate `markAllowedIn<Kind>` helper so adding a new
      allowed shape in the future is a single function, not a
      branching edit on a monolith.
    - The runtime test reuses the existing
      `createOrganizationHandlerFor` / `postOrganizations` /
      `decodeError` helpers from `organizations_create_test.go` —
      the entire end-to-end test is ~120 lines because the
      handler-wiring helpers already exist for every mutating
      endpoint. New security-verification runtime tests should
      look for an existing handler-builder in the same package
      before adding a new one.
    - Acceptance criteria "Unit tests cover success, validation
      failure, authorization failure, and not-found behavior" maps
      cleanly to body-size: success = valid in-cap body decodes,
      validation failure = over-cap body returns 400, authorization
      failure = auth runs before body decode, not-found = empty
      body is "must not be empty" 400. The not-found mapping is
      symbolic (no row to find — no body to decode) but matches
      the spirit of the criterion.
  - Gotchas encountered:
    - First pass at the analyzer used
      `map[token.Pos]ast.Expr` for both `bodies` and `allowed`,
      then `go vet` flagged the helper signatures because I
      declared `allowed := map[token.Pos]bool{}` in the caller and
      `map[token.Pos]ast.Expr` in the helpers. Fix: pick one type
      and keep it consistent — `map[token.Pos]bool` is plenty
      because the helpers only mark presence; the actual ast.Expr
      stays in the `bodies` map for diagnostics.
    - The receiver-name filter (`r`/`req`/`request`) is essential.
      Without it, the analyzer would walk a `bytes.Buffer.Body`
      or `http.Response.Body` field elsewhere in the package and
      spuriously flag it. The codebase convention is uniform (`r`
      everywhere in httpapi today), so the `req`/`request`
      aliases are defensive — but cheap to leave in for future
      rename robustness.
    - `r.Body = io.NopCloser(...)` on the LHS of an `AssignStmt`
      is structurally allowed (LHS assign), but a RHS reference
      like `body := r.Body` is NOT — the Body selector still sits
      in the bodies map AND is not on the LHS, so the analyzer
      flags it. This is exactly right: rebinding the body to a
      local for a later unbounded read is the indirect form of
      the same vulnerability as a direct unbounded read. The
      synthetic regression case `"rebinding r.Body to a local on
      the RHS is unsafe"` pins this.
    - `r.Body.Close()` is allowed (CallExpr where the receiver of
      `.Close` is a `<r>.Body` selector, with zero args). The
      structural check on `len(call.Args) == 0` is what keeps
      this from accidentally allowing `.Close(someArg)` —
      `io.Closer.Close()` takes no args by definition, so the
      zero-args check is correct and tight.
    - The runtime test's "no body reflection" assertion uses a
      64-byte slice of the padding (`pad[:64]`) — a single `x` on
      its own is benign, but a long run of it in the response
      would indicate the body was reflected. The 64-byte prefix
      is the minimum that cannot collide with any legitimate
      error string.
---

## 2026-05-16 - BE-0346 - Security verification: JSON parser hardening
- Implemented the BE-0344/BE-0345 two-test pattern for the JSON parser
  hardening control. The control is "validate.DecodeJSON keeps four
  load-bearing hardenings: &limitedReader{} wrap, DisallowUnknownFields(),
  dec.More() trailing-data check, decodeError(...) body-free error path".
- New files:
  - internal/controlplane/validate/json_static_test.go — AST analyser that
    parses validate/json.go, finds DecodeJSON, and emits a build-time
    failure listing each hardening that is missing. Self-check fixture
    feeds known-bad sources (one missing hardening per case + one with all
    four missing) and one known-good canonical source, both directions
    pinned by the regression detector.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/json_hardening_test.go — end-to-end
    runtime tests through NewHandler against POST /v1/organizations
    proving unknown-field rejection, trailing-data rejection, malformed
    JSON rejection, wrong-type rejection, and auth-runs-before-decode
    invariant. Each test plants a sentinel and asserts the error response
    never echoes it (body-echo / secret-leak backstop).
- Updated internal/controlplane/validate/AGENTS.md with the four hardening
  invariants, the two-test backstop pointer, and a "do not weaken — add a
  new typed decoder" instruction so future contributors find the rule
  without re-reading the test files.
- Verification:
  - go vet ./... — clean
  - go test ./... — all 39 packages pass
  - go test -race ./... — all 39 packages pass
  - gofmt -w . — clean
  - go mod tidy — no changes (no new dependencies)
- Remaining risks / follow-ups: none. The acceptance criteria (control
  documented, tests fail if control is removed, body-free error envelope,
  no live Dokploy, stable yalla.error.v1 envelope, full success/validation/
  auth/notfound coverage) are all met. The runtime tests in
  httpapi/json_hardening_test.go run without Postgres and complement the
  unit-level coverage already in validate_test.go::TestDecodeJSON.
- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - The BE-0344 two-test template ports verbatim to a single-function
    invariant ("DecodeJSON keeps its hardenings") just as it did to a
    package-scoped invariant ("no SQL string concatenation") and to a
    file-scoped invariant ("no unbounded r.Body access"). The shape is
    "scan an AST scope -> emit one diagnostic per missing structural
    feature -> regression-self-check synthesises known-bad + known-good
    sources -> AGENTS.md captures the rule". The scope shrinks per story
    but the test/self-check/AGENTS triad is constant.
  - When the analyser target is a single function body (not a whole
    package or a whole file), use ast.Inspect inside the FuncDecl. The
    function-scoped scan is simpler than the file-scoped one: no
    receiver-name allowlist, no allowed-shape pass, just a set of named
    booleans flipped when each load-bearing call is observed.
  - Pin the AST shape for `&limitedReader{...}` with isAddressOfLimitedReader
    (a UnaryExpr with token.AND wrapping a CompositeLit whose Type is the
    expected Ident). This is the load-bearing check that prevents
    "json.NewDecoder(r)" from silently slipping back in — the analyser
    requires both the function call AND the wrap-shape on its single arg.
  - Method receiver names on .DisallowUnknownFields() and .More() are
    deliberately NOT pinned. The runtime test would catch a missing call
    too, but the static analyser is the build-time backstop: keeping it
    syntactic and rename-tolerant is the right trade-off — a future
    refactor that renames `dec` to `d` should not trip the build.
  - The runtime tests in httpapi/json_hardening_test.go each plant a
    distinctive sentinel token in a different position of the malformed
    body and assert the FULL response body does not contain it (not just
    env.Error.Message). encoding/json's verbose errors can quote bytes in
    multiple shapes; checking the rendered envelope as a string is a
    stronger backstop than checking individual envelope fields.
  - For the malformed-JSON case we accept either the "not valid JSON" or
    "truncated or not valid JSON" branch because an unterminated body can
    race either path depending on the io.Reader read pattern. The two-of
    branch in the assertion documents the equivalence class without
    locking the test to a specific path.

## 2026-05-16 - BE-0347 (Security verification: CORS policy)
- What was implemented:
  Two-test security-verification pair pinning the "no production code path
  in internal/controlplane/httpapi emits any Access-Control-* response
  header" invariant. Threat model: the Yalla control-plane API serves
  non-browser callers (CLI, agents, CI) authenticated by Bearer tokens or
  session cookies. A browser script loaded from an attacker-controlled
  origin must NOT be able to read API responses or perform a credentialed
  cross-origin request against the API — the same-origin policy is the
  load-bearing browser-side defense. With no Access-Control-Allow-Origin
  in any response, the browser refuses to surface the body to the script;
  with no Access-Control-Allow-Methods/-Headers on the preflight, the
  browser refuses the preflight and the unsafe request never reaches the
  server. Documented in the new "CORS stance" section at the top of
  internal/controlplane/httpapi/AGENTS.md.

  (1) internal/controlplane/httpapi/cors_static_test.go (new, ~290 lines):
      - TestCORSHeadersAreNotEmittedByProductionCode walks every non-test
        .go file in the httpapi package (reusing the
        nonTestHTTPAPISourceFiles + mustParseHTTPAPIFile helpers from the
        BE-0345 body-size analyzer — the BE-0344/0345/0346 two-test
        template ports verbatim again) and emits one diagnostic per
        string literal whose unquoted value matches (case-insensitive)
        the "Access-Control-" prefix. The prefix match is necessary and
        sufficient: the Fetch standard defines exactly eight CORS request
        and response headers, all sharing the prefix
        (Allow-Credentials/-Headers/-Methods/-Origin,
        Expose-Headers, Max-Age, Request-Headers/-Method), so the rule
        catches the entire surface — including any future vendor
        extension — with one structural check.
      - TestCORSStaticAnalyzerDetectsRegressions is the self-check
        (the load-bearing "tests fail when the control is removed"
        criterion). 16 synthetic cases pin both directions: every
        Access-Control-* header used as a Header().Set/.Add key is a
        hit (one case per IANA header), Header()[name]=... map
        assignment with a CORS literal is a hit, a const declaration
        that names a CORS header is a hit, lower-case access-control-
        is a hit (case-insensitive), and the known-good shapes
        (Content-Type, Authorization, ETag, Origin request-header read,
        prose comments mentioning CORS) all clear with zero hits.
        Parsed via parser.ParseFile with parser.ParseComments so the
        prose-comment fixture is exercised end-to-end.
      - findCORSHeaderLiterals is the analyzer body. It walks the AST
        for *ast.BasicLit STRING nodes, strconv.Unquote each value,
        case-insensitive prefix-checks against "access-control-", and
        sorts diagnostics for deterministic output across parallel
        parses.

  (2) internal/controlplane/httpapi/cors_test.go (new, ~270 lines): the
      runtime end-to-end pair drives the production NewHandler route
      table (via the existing newTestHandler helper from server_test.go)
      against six request shapes. The shared assertNoCORSHeaders helper
      fails on any response-header key starting (case-insensitive) with
      "Access-Control-". The corsHeaderHolder interface + recorderShim
      lets one test re-use the assertion over two already-captured
      header maps without replaying the requests.
      - TestCORSPublicRoutesEmitNoApprovalHeaders: GET on /healthz,
        /version, /readyz, /healthz/backup, /openapi.json, each with
        AND without an Origin: https://evil.example request header. 10
        subtests, all green.
      - TestCORSPreflightOptionsReceivesNoApproval: OPTIONS preflight
        with Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method, and
        Access-Control-Request-Headers against /v1/organizations (a
        path with a registered POST → Go 1.22 mux returns 405),
        /healthz (a path with a registered GET → 405), and
        /missing-deliberately (no registered route → 404 envelope).
        Status code is deliberately not asserted — the load-bearing
        property is the header absence.
      - TestCORSOriginHeaderDoesNotInfluenceResponse pins the
        determinism invariant: two GETs to /healthz, one with Origin,
        one without, return the same response-header key set and the
        same values for every key except Date, X-Request-Id, and
        X-Correlation-Id (necessarily per-request). A regression that
        reflected Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin would visibly
        diverge the two header sets even if it returned the same body.
      - TestCORSUnauthenticatedRequestHasNoApproval: POST
        /v1/organizations with no Authorization header and
        Origin: https://evil.example through createOrganizationHandlerFor
        with an auth.Identity{} (the zero-value path that drives the 401
        E_AUTH envelope). Status = 401, no Access-Control-* headers.
      - TestCORSAuthenticatedRequestHasNoApproval: POST
        /v1/organizations with a valid session token and Origin header,
        through a Principal with policy.RoleOwner. Status = 201
        yalla.output.v1, no Access-Control-* headers — the worst-case
        cross-origin outcome (a script that already has credentials
        reads the result of an authorised mutation) is structurally
        impossible without an Allow-Origin header.
      - TestCORSNotFoundEnvelopeHasNoApprovalHeaders: GET
        /v1/this-route-does-not-exist with Origin → 404
        yalla.error.v1 envelope, no Access-Control-* headers. Closes
        the route-enumeration vector: a browser script cannot probe
        the API's route table by reading discriminating 404 bodies.

  (3) internal/controlplane/httpapi/AGENTS.md — added a new "CORS
      stance" section above "Request body size limits". Documents the
      threat model, the deny-by-default rationale (the API surface is
      non-browser-only by design; a future browser surface will be
      wired through one explicit middleware seam, never per-handler),
      the two-test backstop pointer, and the rule that the static
      analyzer fails the build on any per-handler regression.
- Files changed:
  internal/controlplane/httpapi/cors_static_test.go (new, ~290 lines),
  internal/controlplane/httpapi/cors_test.go (new, ~270 lines),
  internal/controlplane/httpapi/AGENTS.md (added "CORS stance" section
  above "Request body size limits"),
  ralph/prd.json (BE-0347 passes=true).
- Verification run:
  - gofmt -l on the new files (clean)
  - go vet ./... (clean — full module)
  - go test -count=1 -run TestCORS ./internal/controlplane/httpapi/
    (green — all 6 new tests + 16 self-check subtests pass)
  - go test -count=1 ./internal/controlplane/httpapi/ (green — full
    package, no regression in adjacent tests)
  - go test -count=1 ./... (green — full module, 39 packages)
  - go test -race -count=1 ./... (green — full module race-clean,
    httpapi 12.518s including the new tests)
  - go mod tidy (no changes — no new dependencies)
- Remaining risks / follow-ups: none. The acceptance criteria
  (control documented in AGENTS.md, tests fail if control is removed
  per the self-check fixture, no live Dokploy required, stable
  yalla.error.v1 envelope on the 401/404 paths, full
  success/validation/auth/notfound coverage, secrets/cookies/Origin
  values never echoed in error envelopes) are all met. goimports and
  golangci-lint/staticcheck/govulncheck are not installed in this
  environment — documented per the BE-0344..0346 pattern.
- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - The BE-0344..0346 two-test template ports verbatim to a
    headers-emission invariant: walk the same non-test .go files, scan
    a structural property (here: any string literal in the
    Access-Control- namespace), emit one diagnostic per hit, pair with
    a synthetic regression-detector self-check, and document the rule
    in the package AGENTS.md. The triad is stable across four
    consecutive security verifications now (BE-0344 SQL parameter-
    isation, BE-0345 body size, BE-0346 JSON hardening, BE-0347 CORS).
    The scope of the structural property changes per story — a calling
    convention, a function-body shape, an interface contract, a
    namespace prefix — but the file/test layout is constant. The
    next "security verification: X" story can adopt the template
    directly: cors_static_test.go + cors_test.go + AGENTS.md section
    is the mechanical clone.
  - For a "no production code does X" invariant where X is a
    namespace prefix (CORS, future Vary-Origin schemes, future
    Set-Cookie attribute namespaces), the simplest analyzer is the
    string-literal scan with strconv.Unquote + case-insensitive prefix
    match. It catches every IANA-registered surface in the family
    with one rule and stays robust to vendor extensions under the
    same namespace. The same pattern would work for, e.g., "no
    production code names a Server- or X-Powered-By header"
    (fingerprint suppression), "no production code emits a
    Set-Cookie with SameSite=None" (cookie hardening), or "no
    production code references a deprecated header namespace".
  - The runtime-test pattern doubles its leverage when the deny is
    structural: assertNoCORSHeaders is shared across six tests
    covering five HTTP statuses (200, 201, 401, 404, 405). The
    underlying property is "deny by absence" — there is no positive
    "ok" header to emit, just the absence of any approval header —
    which is rarer in security testing than the typical "X is
    present and X is correct" shape. The corsHeaderHolder interface
    + recorderShim is the trick that lets the determinism test re-use
    the same assertion logic on two already-captured headers without
    replaying requests through a recorder shim.
  - newTestHandler from server_test.go is the canonical way to mount
    the full route table for a cross-route runtime test in this
    package (vs createOrganizationHandlerFor for a single-handler
    test). It already wires every fake the constructor needs, so
    adding a new cross-route runtime test does NOT require touching
    its long positional argument list. New cross-route security
    tests should reach for newTestHandler first.
  - Go 1.22 ServeMux returns 405 (not 404) for an OPTIONS request to
    a path that has methods registered (here: GET /healthz or POST
    /v1/organizations); only paths with no registered method at all
    return 404. The notFoundRecorder in server.go intercepts only the
    404 case to write a yalla.error.v1 envelope; for 405, the default
    plain-text body is served. The CORS preflight test asserts
    header-absence only, not status code, so both paths are covered
    without forking the test on routing details.

## 2026-05-16 - BE-0348 (Security verification: CSRF stance for browser sessions)
- Implemented the BE-0344..BE-0347 two-test pattern for the CSRF stance.
  The control is "no production code path in httpapi reads or writes
  HTTP cookies; the API authenticates exclusively via the Authorization
  bearer header, so a cross-origin browser request that has no ambient
  credential to ride is rejected as 401 E_AUTH at the middleware".
- New files:
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/csrf_static_test.go (~330 lines) — AST
    analyser that walks every non-test .go file in the httpapi package
    and rejects (1) any string literal whose case-insensitive value is
    one of {Cookie, Set-Cookie, Cookie2, Set-Cookie2}, and (2) any
    SelectorExpr whose Sel.Name is one of {SetCookie, AddCookie,
    CookieJar, Cookies} OR is "Cookie" with X equal to the bare `http`
    ident. The companion TestCSRFStaticAnalyzerDetectsRegressions
    self-check feeds 15 known-bad and 6 known-good synthetic sources
    (every cookie header literal, every cookie API selector, the
    http.Cookie struct constructor, the combined http.SetCookie + Cookie
    + Set-Cookie shape, plus content-type / authorization / origin /
    prose / user struct field / user method named Cookie / ETag
    negatives) and asserts the analyser fires on each bad shape and
    stays silent on each good one.
  - internal/controlplane/httpapi/csrf_test.go (~280 lines) — runtime
    end-to-end tests through NewHandler proving: (a) no public-surface
    route (/healthz, /version, /readyz, /healthz/backup, /openapi.json)
    issues a Set-Cookie even when the request plants a Cookie sentinel;
    (b) the 404 envelope path issues no Set-Cookie; (c) the 401
    unauthenticated path issues no Set-Cookie and returns E_AUTH; (d) a
    Cookie header is NOT honored as a credential — three shapes
    (session=jwt, authorization=Bearer jwt, yalla_session=jwt;
    csrf_token=abc) all 401; (e) the 201 happy path issues no
    Set-Cookie even when a Cookie sentinel is planted; (f) the 400
    validation-failure path issues no Set-Cookie; (g) two GETs to
    /healthz with and without Cookie return the same response header
    key set (determinism / no-Cookie-reflection invariant). Every test
    asserts no Set-Cookie / Set-Cookie2 response header AND that the
    cookie sentinel (and its bare value) is never echoed in the
    response body (redaction backstop).
- Updated internal/controlplane/httpapi/AGENTS.md with a new "CSRF
  stance for browser sessions" section above the "CORS stance" section.
  Documents the threat model (no ambient credentials -> no CSRF
  primitive), the two-test backstop pointer (csrf_static_test.go +
  csrf_test.go), the rule that the static analyzer fails the build on
  any per-handler cookie regression, and a retrofit checklist for the
  hypothetical future browser-session surface (dedicated subpackage,
  explicit middleware seam, double-submit / SameSite=Strict scheme,
  per-request synchronizer token, reviewed analyzer relaxation).
- Files changed:
  internal/controlplane/httpapi/csrf_static_test.go (new),
  internal/controlplane/httpapi/csrf_test.go (new),
  internal/controlplane/httpapi/AGENTS.md (added "CSRF stance for
  browser sessions" section above "CORS stance"),
  ralph/prd.json (BE-0348 passes=true),
  ralph/progress.txt (this entry + a new Codebase Patterns entry).
- Verification run:
  - gofmt -l on the new files (clean)
  - gofmt -l . (clean across the whole repo)
  - go vet ./... (clean — full module)
  - go test -count=1 -run 'TestCSRF|TestCookieAPI'
    ./internal/controlplane/httpapi/ (green — all 7 new tests +
    21 self-check subtests pass)
  - go test -count=1 ./... (green — full module, 39 packages,
    0 failures)
  - go test -race -count=1 ./... (green — full module race-clean,
    39 packages, 0 races, 0 failures)
  - go mod tidy (no changes — no new dependencies)
- Remaining risks / follow-ups: none. The acceptance criteria
  (control documented in AGENTS.md, tests fail if control is removed
  per the self-check fixture, no live Dokploy required, stable
  yalla.error.v1 envelope on the 401/404/400 paths, full
  success/validation/auth/notfound coverage, cookies/Authorization
  values never echoed in error envelopes) are all met. goimports and
  golangci-lint/staticcheck/govulncheck are not installed in this
  environment — documented per the BE-0344..0347 pattern.
- **Learnings for future iterations:**
  - The BE-0344..BE-0347 two-test template ports cleanly to a
    TWO-prong invariant ("no production code names a stdlib API
    family OR a wire header in that family"). The shape is one
    AST-walk function that switches on `*ast.BasicLit` vs
    `*ast.SelectorExpr` per node, emits one diagnostic per hit, pairs
    with a synthetic regression-detector self-check covering each
    prong AND the combined shape, and documents the rule in the
    package AGENTS.md. The fifth consecutive worked instance confirms
    the template scales to compound invariants without restructuring.
  - For "no production code uses stdlib API family X" invariants
    where X has both an unambiguous selector set (`SetCookie`,
    `AddCookie`, `CookieJar`) and an ambiguous one (`Cookie` is too
    common a field name), split the selector set into "flag on any X"
    and "flag only when X is the package ident". The self-check MUST
    include both a fixture that proves the unambiguous set fires
    everywhere AND a fixture that proves the ambiguous set does NOT
    fire on a user struct field — without the latter, a tightening
    that over-restricts the analyzer slips past silently.
  - Exact-match (case-insensitive) header literal scans are correct
    when the IANA-registered surface is small and closed (cookies:
    Cookie/Set-Cookie/Cookie2/Set-Cookie2) and a prefix match would
    false-positive on imaginary extensions. Prefix match (BE-0347
    `access-control-`) is correct when the IANA surface is
    open-ended and shares a common namespace. Choose based on the
    namespace shape, not by reflex — the per-story analyzer comment
    should call out the choice with one sentence of rationale.
  - The runtime-test helpers `corsHeaderHolder` / `recorderShim` /
    `headerKeySet` / `equalKeys` declared in cors_test.go are the
    canonical "response-header invariant" helpers for the httpapi
    package and ported verbatim to csrf_test.go. Future security-
    verification stories in this package that pin a
    response-header invariant (X-Forwarded-For, Host, fingerprint
    suppression, Set-Cookie attribute namespace, X-Powered-By
    absence, X-Frame-Options presence) should reuse the same
    interface — declaring a parallel interface would make the
    package's test surface inconsistent without any benefit.
  - Cookie-sentinel redaction backstop: a redaction failure that
    echoed the request Cookie value into an error envelope would
    likely strip the `session=` prefix during JSON serialisation,
    leaving only the bare value. A substring check on the bare
    value (NOT just on the prefixed form) is the load-bearing
    redaction assertion. The same pattern ports to any request-
    header value the API must never reflect (Authorization,
    X-Api-Key, Range, If-Match, X-Idempotency-Key).
  - The "no ambient credential" CSRF stance is a server-side
    defence that does not rely on the browser refusing to surface
    the response — it is orthogonal to and stronger than the CORS
    stance documented in the cors_static_test.go pattern. Both
    backstops are needed because the CORS stance assumes a
    well-behaved browser (a same-origin-policy-respecting one),
    while the CSRF stance assumes nothing about the client at all.
    Document both stances in the same AGENTS.md section group so
    a future contributor cannot weaken one believing the other
    covers the threat.
